prs.title: fix(beam): avoid blocking mirror cleanup on a captured response tee
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Beam mirror upload runs while diagnostic HTTP capture is enabled (`OPENCLAW_DEBUG_PROXY_ENABLED=1`) and the receiver responds slowly, the upload's cleanup stalls and the connection slot stays unreturned for up to 10 seconds per poll retry. The `finally` block in `createBeamMirrorRunner`'s upload path discards the ignored response body with `await response.body?.cancel()`, but capture has already tee'd the response through `response.clone()`, so awaiting the caller's branch cancel waits for the capture branch to settle (bounded by the capture reader's 10s idle deadline). The dispatcher `release()` that reclaims the connection slot sits behind that wait — exactly the "retain connection slots across poll retries" outcome the adjacent comment says the cancel exists to prevent.

- Problem: `extensions/beam/src/mirror.ts` awaited the caller's tee-branch cancel before releasing the dispatcher, so a held capture branch delayed cleanup on every upload poll retry.
- Solution: fire-and-forget the cancel (`void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`), matching the canonical owner `cancelUnreadResponseBody`, then release the dispatcher in `finally` exactly as before.
- What changed: one word in the upload `finally`; the existing lifecycle-abort regression test now holds the cancel to model a live capture tee branch.
- What did NOT change: the `finally { await release() }` ordering (shutdown still waits for guarded cleanup), the cancel being initiated on every path, redirect blocking, throttled warnings, timeouts, and every behavior with capture disabled (the default).

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adopts the repository's canonical form for discarding an unread, possibly-tee'd response body. `cancelUnreadResponseBody` (`src/infra/http-response-body.ts:10`) documents the invariant — "A capture tee must not delay errors or the caller's bounded dispatcher release" — and implements it as `void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`. The same form was merged for the marketplace capture path in #191675 and is under review for the xAI OAuth challenge path in #198219; the Beam mirror call site was a remaining caller that awaited the cancel directly. An extension cannot import the core owner file (plugin boundary), so the call site adopts the owner's expression verbatim. The nearest in-extension precedent states the reason outright — `extensions/feishu/src/streaming-card.ts:83` keeps a local copy of the helper with the comment "Do not await: debug capture can tee the stream and deadlock a waiter."

Best fix: yes. It reuses the established owner form rather than adding a new guard, and keeps the production change to a single word. Alternative considered: passing `capture: false` for the mirror upload fetch; rejected because it would remove diagnostic visibility for mirror traffic and diverge from the owner-level invariant that callers must not await a tee-branch cancel. Risk: the cancel is now best-effort, but the dispatcher release still aborts the request controller and closes the transport, so the unread body is reclaimed by the existing release path.

## User Impact

Operators running Beam session mirroring with diagnostic capture enabled no longer have a slow receiver hold a dispatcher connection slot (up to 10s) between upload polls: cleanup releases the slot immediately while the ignored body is still being discarded. With capture disabled (the default), the cancel already resolved instantly and behavior is unchanged. Service shutdown still waits for the guarded response release to finish before settling.

## Evidence

| Mirror-upload cleanup metric | Before (`await cancel()`, origin/main) | After (`void cancel()`, this head) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shipped built Gateway running the real Beam mirror service, capture on, receiver holds the body 3000 ms — transport closed after response headers | 3023 / 3006 / 3003 ms | 15 / 4 / 4 / 4 ms |
| Shipped, capture on — transport still closed before the held body drained (`closedBeforeBodyRelease`) | false on every in-run upload | true on all 4 uploads |
| Shipped, capture disabled (the default) — same measurement | 30 / 2 / 2 ms (inert) | 50 / 2 / 3 ms (inert) |
| Real mirror POSTs delivered per run (receiver-recorded request bodies) | 4 | 4 |
| Guarded-fetch transport call in isolation, capture on — dispatcher `release()` reached after | 2993 / 2996 / 2999 ms | 0 / 0 / 0 ms |
| Committed regression (held capture-tee cancel) at the real Beam call site | FAIL — `Error: Test timed out in 120000ms` | PASS |
| Cancel initiated | once | once (unchanged) |
| Warnings surfaced | none | none (unchanged) |

### Shipped end-to-end: built Gateway running the real Beam mirror service

The built artifact from this head (`dist/index.js`, produced by `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts runtime` in this branch's worktree) was started as a real isolated Gateway — its own scratch `HOME`, state dir, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, config with `plugins.entries.beam.config.mirror` and the anthropic native session catalog — by a `node` harness that also:

- synthesizes a Claude-style transcript in the catalog's explicit project root and appends a turn every 8 s, so each 10 s poll produces a new fingerprint instead of a deduplicated no-op;
- runs a local `node:http` receiver as the mirror endpoint that flushes `200` + `{"ok":true` and then holds the rest of the JSON body open for 3000 ms, recording per request when the client's transport closed relative to that held release;
- sets `OPENCLAW_DEBUG_PROXY_ENABLED=1` so the guarded fetch really tees the response through the capture branch (`src/proxy-capture/runtime-response-body.ts:140-161`).

The before cells are the *same built file* with only the one-word cancel form restored (`await c.body?.cancel()…`), and each output echoes the snippet it actually ran (`distCancelForm`), so the two forms cannot be confused:

After (this head):

```console
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .artifacts/beam-shipped-mirror-proof.mts  # LABEL=head CAPTURE=1 UPLOADS=4 HOLD_MS=3000
{"label":"head","captureEnabled":true,"holdMs":3000,"uploadsSeen":4,"distCancelForm":".ok}finally{c.body?.cancel().catch(()=>void 0);await l()}}","root":"/tmp/beam-shipped-H8xy0R","uploads":[{"bytes":449,"closeDelayMs":15,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":512,"closeDelayMs":4,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":574,"closeDelayMs":4,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":699,"closeDelayMs":4,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true}]}
```

Before (origin/main cancel form):

```console
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .artifacts/beam-shipped-mirror-proof.mts  # LABEL=base CAPTURE=1 UPLOADS=4 HOLD_MS=3000
{"label":"base","captureEnabled":true,"holdMs":3000,"uploadsSeen":4,"distCancelForm":"nally{await c.body?.cancel().catch(()=>void 0);await l()}}","root":"/tmp/beam-shipped-hnCYEh","uploads":[{"bytes":449,"closeDelayMs":3023,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false},{"bytes":574,"closeDelayMs":3006,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false},{"bytes":637,"closeDelayMs":3003,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false},{"bytes":762,"closeDelayMs":57,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true}]}
```

`closeDelayMs` is measured on the receiver: headers arrived, then the connection stayed open for the whole 3000 ms body hold in the before cells, while the after cells close within 4-15 ms of the response — the mirror's `finally` reached `release()` while the receiver still held the body. Both runs log the same real upload path (`beam mirror active: claude -> http://127.0.0.1:<port>`) and deliver 4 real POST bodies (449-762 bytes). The last before-cell row (`57 ms`) is the harness's own teardown: the loop stops and sends `SIGTERM` as soon as it observes the requested upload count, so that final exchange's close is shutdown-driven rather than cleanup-driven; the same truncation does not appear in the after cells because their cleanup never waits.

Control with capture disabled (the shipped default) — both forms close in single-digit tens of milliseconds, so the change is inert unless diagnostic capture is on:

```console
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .artifacts/beam-shipped-mirror-proof.mts  # LABEL=base CAPTURE=0 UPLOADS=4 HOLD_MS=3000
{"label":"base","captureEnabled":false,"holdMs":3000,"uploadsSeen":4,"distCancelForm":"nally{await c.body?.cancel().catch(()=>void 0);await l()}}","root":"/tmp/beam-shipped-6PwtMp","uploads":[{"bytes":449,"closeDelayMs":30,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":512,"closeDelayMs":2,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":574,"closeDelayMs":2,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":699,"closeDelayMs":2,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true}]}
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .artifacts/beam-shipped-mirror-proof.mts  # LABEL=head CAPTURE=0 UPLOADS=4 HOLD_MS=3000
{"label":"head","captureEnabled":false,"holdMs":3000,"uploadsSeen":4,"distCancelForm":".ok}finally{c.body?.cancel().catch(()=>void 0);await l()}}","root":"/tmp/beam-shipped-tmrSqh","uploads":[{"bytes":449,"closeDelayMs":50,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":574,"closeDelayMs":2,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":637,"closeDelayMs":3,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"bytes":699,"closeDelayMs":1,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true}]}
```

### Dispatcher-release timing at the transport call

The same invariant was measured from inside the cleanup block itself: the mirror upload's transport call (`fetchWithSsrFGuard` with the mirror's own `url` / `timeoutMs` / `policy` / `auditContext: "beam.mirror_upload"` / `maxRedirects: 0` / POST body) and its `finally` replayed verbatim in a standalone `node` run against a real loopback receiver that holds the body open for 3000 ms, with the same capture flag. Only the cancel form differs between runs.

After (this head) — `void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` then `await release()`; `bodyStillHeldAtRelease: true` is the discriminator, the slot is reclaimed while the receiver still holds the body:

```console
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs beam-cancel-tee-proof.mts  # FORM=head CAPTURE=1 UPLOADS=3 HOLD_MS=3000
{"form":"head","captureEnabled":true,"holdMs":3000,"uploads":3,"rows":[{"upload":1,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":17,"releaseReachedAfterMs":0,"releaseElapsedMs":17,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":true,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000},{"upload":2,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":2,"releaseReachedAfterMs":0,"releaseElapsedMs":2,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":true,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000},{"upload":3,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":1,"releaseReachedAfterMs":0,"releaseElapsedMs":1,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":true,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000}]}
```

Before (origin/main) — the same run with `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`, so `release()` is reached only after the held capture branch settles:

```console
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs beam-cancel-tee-proof.mts  # FORM=base CAPTURE=1 UPLOADS=3 HOLD_MS=3000
{"form":"base","captureEnabled":true,"holdMs":3000,"uploads":3,"rows":[{"upload":1,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":3003,"releaseReachedAfterMs":2993,"releaseElapsedMs":10,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":false,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000},{"upload":2,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":2997,"releaseReachedAfterMs":2996,"releaseElapsedMs":1,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":false,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000},{"upload":3,"result":true,"cleanupElapsedMs":3001,"releaseReachedAfterMs":2999,"releaseElapsedMs":2,"bodyStillHeldAtRelease":false,"receiverHeldBodyMs":3000}]}
```

With a longer hold the awaited form blocks up to the capture read idle bound (10s, `CAPTURED_RESPONSE_BODY_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`); the held-for-3s case was chosen so one run stays inside the 15s upload timeout.

### Committed regression at the real product call site

The existing lifecycle-abort test in `extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts` ("forwards lifecycle abort and waits for guarded response cleanup without warning") was extended so the response body's `cancel` returns a promise that never settles — structurally identical to a live capture tee branch holding the caller's side of the tee (no wall-clock assumptions). On origin/main production code the upload's `finally` awaits that cancel and never reaches `release()`, so the test's cleanup barrier never starts and the test times out; on this head the cancel is initiated and discarded, `release()` runs immediately, and the same assertions (cleanup started while cancel is still pending, shutdown settles only after the release barrier completes, cancel invoked exactly once, no warnings) all pass.

RED — base production code (byte-identical `origin/main` file) with the extended test:

```console
$ vitest run extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts -t "forwards lifecycle abort"
 FAIL   extensions  extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts > createBeamMirrorRunner > forwards lifecycle abort and waits for guarded response cleanup without warning
Error: Test timed out in 120000ms.
 ❯ extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts:258:3

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 19 skipped (20)
   Duration  169.11s
```

GREEN — this head, full file:

```console
$ vitest run extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  20 passed (20)
   Start at  07:46:16
   Duration  14.08s
```

### Corroboration on the sibling call site of this anchor

The same owner-form fix under the same anchor was measured end-to-end in a shipped product session for the xAI marketplace capture path in sibling PR #198219 (real `openclaw models list --refresh` CLI child process over real TLS through a local capture proxy: transport closed in 4-14ms with the body held versus ~3005ms without the fix), and the merged precedent #191675 established the owner form. This PR applies that fix to the remaining Beam mirror call site, with the Beam-specific shipped matrix and committed regression above.

What was not tested:

- The shipped cells drive the real `createBeamMirrorRunner` service (activation, poll scan, catalog read, fingerprint dedup, guarded POST upload, cleanup) inside a built Gateway, but the mirrored transcript is a synthetic Claude-format JSONL file and the receiver credential is a synthetic bearer token; no operator's real Beam endpoint or real conversation data was involved. The guarded-fetch transport, the diagnostic capture tee, the dispatcher release and the cancel paths all run unmodified.
- The final upload of the before/capture-on cell is closed early by the harness's own `SIGTERM` teardown (the loop stops at the requested upload count), so it reads 57 ms instead of ~3000 ms; the three in-run uploads carry the before/after comparison and the after cells are unaffected by the same teardown.
- A hold longer than the capture read idle bound (10s) was not run live, because the 15s upload timeout would make the two forms differ only by which error they surface; the bounded-stall behavior is the capture owner's existing contract, unchanged here.
- Local `oxlint` could not run in this environment at all: its config loads `./tools/solid-lint/index.mjs`, which imports `eslint-plugin-solid`, and that package is a dangling symlink in the local install (`node_modules/eslint-plugin-solid` -> an unmaterialized `.pnpm` entry). Lint therefore relies on CI `check-lint`. `oxfmt` and the affected test suites were run locally and are clean (`git diff --check` empty; `extensions/beam/src/mirror.test.ts` + `mirror-retry.test.ts` = 23 passed).

### Open PR collision check

Swept against the submission-day open-PR snapshot two ways. Changed files: the 60 most recently updated open PRs were enumerated with their file lists and none touches `extensions/beam/*` at all, let alone `extensions/beam/src/mirror.ts` / `mirror.test.ts`. Title/body search: `mirror in:title` returns 6 open PRs (replay admission, telegram final deliveries, usage double-count, plugin-sdk write assertion, imessage echo cache, session mirroring feature) and none of their files include `extensions/beam`; `capture tee` returns this anchor's sibling #198219, which changes only `extensions/xai/*` (zero file overlap). The merged precedent #191675 (`src/plugins/marketplace.ts`) established the owner form, and `origin/main` still has `await response.body?.cancel()` at this call site, so the bug is live and uncovered.

prs.title: fix(xai): avoid blocking OAuth challenge cleanup on a capture tee
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an xAI OAuth refresh is intercepted by a Cloudflare challenge (`403` with `cf-mitigated: challenge`) while diagnostic HTTP capture is enabled (`OPENCLAW_DEBUG_PROXY_ENABLED=1`), the refresh stalls instead of retrying promptly. The challenge handler discards the unread HTML body with `await response.body?.cancel()`, but capture has already tee'd the response through `response.clone()`, so cancelling the caller's branch waits for the capture branch to settle (up to its 10s idle bound). The dispatcher release that follows sits behind that wait, and the retry loop can serialize up to three such stalls in a single refresh.

- Problem: `extensions/xai/xai-oauth.ts` awaited the caller's tee-branch cancel before releasing the dispatcher, so a held capture branch delayed challenge cleanup and retry.
- Solution: fire-and-forget the cancel (`void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`), matching the canonical owner `cancelUnreadResponseBody`, then release the dispatcher in `finally` exactly as before.
- What changed: one line in the verified-challenge branch of `requestXaiOAuthRefresh`; the existing regression test was extended to hold the cancel.
- What did NOT change: the grant-safety semantics (an HTML challenge is not evidence the rotating grant was consumed, and is never replayed), the 3-attempt bound, the `finally { await result.release() }` ordering, and every non-challenge path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adopts the repository's canonical form for discarding an unread, possibly-tee'd response body. `cancelUnreadResponseBody` (`src/infra/http-response-body.ts`) already documents the invariant ("A capture tee must not delay errors or the caller's bounded dispatcher release") and uses `void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`. The same form was merged for the marketplace capture path in #191675. The xAI challenge branch was a remaining caller that awaited the cancel directly.

Best fix: yes. It reuses the established owner form rather than adding a new guard, and keeps the production change to a single line. Alternative considered: disabling capture for the OAuth fetch (`capture: false`); rejected because it would remove diagnostic visibility for the OAuth flow and diverge from the owner-level invariant that callers must not await a tee-branch cancel. Risk: the cancel is now best-effort, but the dispatcher release still aborts the request controller and closes the transport, so the unread body is reclaimed by the existing release path. The grant is never read or replayed on the challenge path, unchanged.

## User Impact

Operators running xAI OAuth refresh or login with diagnostic capture enabled no longer see the refresh hang on a Cloudflare challenge: the challenge body is discarded and retried promptly (up to the existing 3-attempt bound), and a persistent challenge still surfaces the same recoverable "blocked by a Cloudflare challenge; retry later" error. With capture disabled (the default), behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Full product session through the shipped CLI

The real `openclaw models list --refresh` command (built from this head, `f31202c`) is spawned as a child process against an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` seeded with a synthetic expired `xai:default` OAuth credential, written through the canonical `upsertAuthProfileAsync` owner. With no Gateway running, the CLI refreshes the local model catalog: live discovery for the bundled xAI plugin drives the product's auth resolution -> `resolveApiKeyForProvider` -> `refreshOAuth` -> `refreshXaiOAuthCredential` -> the verified Cloudflare challenge. The refresh runs over real TLS through a local MITM forward proxy impersonating `auth.x.ai` behind a trusted CA, with the CLI's own diagnostic capture enabled (`OPENCLAW_DEBUG_PROXY_ENABLED=1`). Each challenge flushes its `403` + `cf-mitigated: challenge` headers immediately and then holds the HTML body for 3s, so the capture clone genuinely tees a live body. The connection-release invariant is measured server-side at the proxy backend (when the client transport closes relative to the held challenge body), independent of CLI startup. Before/after differ only by the PR's one-line cancel form in the built `dist/extensions/xai/xai-oauth.js` (`await o.body?.cancel()` versus `o.body?.cancel().catch(()=>void 0)`); every other byte of the product is identical.

| Shipped-CLI metric (3 verified challenges, capture on, held body 3s) | Before (`await cancel()`, origin/main) | After (`void cancel()`, this head) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transport closed before the held body finished | no — 0/3 (waits out the 3s hold) | yes — 3/3 |
| Connection close delay after challenge headers | 3005 / 3003 / 3002 ms | 14 / 6 / 4 ms |
| Total `models list --refresh` wall-clock | 25254 ms | 16362 ms |
| Refresh attempts reaching the token endpoint | 3 | 3 |
| Diagnostic capture events (request + response tee) | 6 | 6 |
| Surfaced product outcome | recoverable challenge error | recoverable challenge error (unchanged) |

After (this head), the shipped CLI releases each challenge connection within ~4-14ms while the body is still held, retries promptly, and ends in the same recoverable error:

```console
$ LABEL=head-on CAPTURE=1 HOLD_MS=3000 node --import tsx/esm shipped-entry-proof.mts
{"LABEL":"head-on","entry":"openclaw.mjs models list --refresh (shipped CLI child process)","cliElapsedMs":16362,"tokenRequests":3,"closedBeforeBodyReleaseCount":3,"capturedEvents":6,"requests":[{"closeDelayMs":14,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"closeDelayMs":6,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true},{"closeDelayMs":4,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":true}]}
```

Before (origin/main cancel form), the same shipped CLI waits out each 3s hold before releasing the connection:

```console
$ LABEL=base-on CAPTURE=1 HOLD_MS=3000 node --import tsx/esm shipped-entry-proof.mts
{"LABEL":"base-on","entry":"openclaw.mjs models list --refresh (shipped CLI child process)","cliElapsedMs":25254,"tokenRequests":3,"closedBeforeBodyReleaseCount":0,"capturedEvents":6,"requests":[{"closeDelayMs":3005,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false},{"closeDelayMs":3003,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false},{"closeDelayMs":3002,"closedBeforeBodyRelease":false}]}
```

Both runs surface the identical real product diagnostic (catalog discovery reports the unresolved xAI profile and the recoverable challenge), confirming the refresh ran end-to-end inside the product session:

```console
[agents/model-providers] xai: OAuth profile "xai:default" could not be resolved (OAuth token refresh failed for xai: xAI OAuth refresh blocked by a Cloudflare challenge; retry later. Please try again or re-authenticate.); no live provider catalog was returned. Re-authenticate with openclaw models auth login --provider xai --profile-id 'xai:default' --agent 'main'.
```

`capturedEvents=6` (3 requests + 3 responses) in both runs confirms the diagnostic capture genuinely tees each challenge response inside the product session. The awaited cancel (before) blocks on that held tee branch, so the transport closes only after the body drains (~3000ms); the fire-and-forget cancel (after) lets `finally { await result.release() }` run immediately, closing the transport in ~4-14ms before the held body finishes. `closedBeforeBodyRelease` is the discriminator. Both runs end in the same recoverable challenge error with the grant untouched.

### Committed regression at the real credential owner

The fold-in regression holds the response body's cancel to model a held capture tee branch and runs the real credential owner code path (3 verified challenges):

| Case | Before (`await cancel()`, origin/main) | After (`void cancel()`, this head) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Held capture-tee branch, 3 verified challenges | hangs, test timed out in 8000ms | settles in 815ms, grant recovered |
| Null-body challenge, no tee (control) | 590ms, 3 retries, recoverable error | 523ms, 3 retries, recoverable error (unchanged) |

Pre-fix RED (production line reverted to `await response.body?.cancel()`, test kept):

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts extensions/xai/xai-oauth.test.ts -t "retries only verified|bounds repeated verified" --testTimeout=8000
 x  xAI OAuth > retries only verified Cloudflare challenge headers without reading the challenge body or waiting for a capture tee 8219ms
   -> Test timed out in 8000ms.
 ok xAI OAuth > bounds repeated verified challenges and leaves the unconsumed grant recoverable 590ms
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 1 passed | 46 skipped (48)
```

Post-fix GREEN (this head):

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts extensions/xai/xai-oauth.test.ts -t "retries only verified|bounds repeated verified" --testTimeout=8000

 ok xAI OAuth > bounds repeated verified challenges and leaves the unconsumed grant recoverable 523ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed | 46 skipped (48)
```

### Real-transport owner corroboration (including a hold that outlasts the capture idle bound)

The same MITM proxy, real TLS and real capture were also driven directly at the shipped owner `refreshXaiOAuthCredential`, with call-through (log-only) wraps on undici's `ProxyAgent` `close`/`destroy` to time dispatcher cleanup; transport, TLS, proxy, capture and retry all run unmodified. This corroborates the product-session result and adds a 12s hold that outlasts the 10s capture idle bound:

| Real-transport owner metric (3 verified challenges, capture on) | Before (`await cancel()`, origin/main) | After (`void cancel()`, this head) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Held body 3s: total refresh wall-clock | 9734ms | 670ms |
| Held body 3s: dispatcher cleanup after challenge headers | ~3007ms | ~19ms |
| Held body 12s (outlasts the 10s capture idle): total refresh | 30692ms | 695ms |
| Held body 12s: dispatcher cleanup after challenge headers | ~10024ms | ~6-28ms |

At the 12s hold the capture idle bound (10s) fires before the body, so the discriminator there is the dispatcher-cleanup latency (~10024ms before versus ~6-28ms after); `capturedEvents=6` in every run. Both forms end in the same recoverable challenge error with the grant untouched.

What was not tested:
- No live xAI account or real Cloudflare challenge was used. The challenge is synthesized (`403` + `cf-mitigated: challenge`) and the credential is synthetic; the real product session (shipped CLI catalog discovery), the real credential owner code path, and real TLS transport run in every proof.

The canonical owner form is already merged (#191675, marketplace path). The only open PR touching this test file is #178840 (device-code poll-loop test hygiene near the end of the file), which is unrelated to the challenge-cancel branch and does not touch the production file. prs.title: fix(doctor): surface pairing store read failures in allowlist repair
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw doctor --fix` silently swallowed pairing-store read failures in `maybeRepairAllowlistPolicyAllowFrom`: `.catch(() => [])` made a failed read look like "no entries", so allowlist recovery was skipped with no operator-visible diagnostic.

The earlier revision reported that diagnostic through `changes`. That is wrong: `applyMutation` treats non-empty `changes` as a candidate-config mutation, requests a config write, and queues the message as a config-change panel even though no allowlist entry was restored.

## Why This Change Was Made

`runDoctorRepairSequence` already consumes a separate `warnings` channel (`appendNotes(warningNotes, mutation.warnings)`) and renders it as an independent "Doctor warnings" panel. The repair now returns an optional `warnings` array, keeps `changes` empty unless senders were really restored, and leaves the healthy return shape unchanged. No new type, export, schema field, or runtime mechanism is added.

The message states the outcome and the next action: recovery was skipped, retry `openclaw doctor --fix`, then run `openclaw doctor` to repair the state database. Error text goes through `formatErrorMessage` instead of raw `String(err)`.

## User Impact

Operators see the failure under `Doctor warnings` even when no config is written, and get a retry/recovery path. Doctor no longer queues a phantom config change. Healthy reads behave exactly as before.

## Evidence

### Upgrade run: released v2026.11.3 state and config, then candidate

State directory and `openclaw.json` were produced by the shipped v2026.11.3 CLI in an isolated `HOME`, then two pairing rows were inserted into the released-version `channel_pairing_allow_entries` table (the same row shape the app writes). The candidate head loaded that same state and ran the shipped CLI:

```console
released arm:  openclaw --version  ->  OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (847611d)
state schema:  user_version 22 (released)  ->  40 (candidate)
$ node --import tsx src/entry.ts doctor --fix --non-interactive
◇  Doctor changes
│  - channels.signal.allowFrom: restored 1 sender entry from pairing    │
│    store (dmPolicy="allowlist").
```

Config diff before -> after (senders redacted):

```console
channels.signal.allowFrom      : []     -> ["+86***1111"]
channels.signal.groupAllowFrom : absent -> ["+86***1111"]
meta.migrations.*, wizard.lastRun*: version bookkeeping only
```

Every other setting (agents, plugins, channel options) is unchanged, and the schema-22 to schema-40 migration preserved both pairing rows. A control arm built with the same released-version steps restores the same sender with exit 0, so the healthy path is unchanged. On the candidate the process exits 1 later at `plugin-doctor-post-session-state` with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` (`unicorn-magic`) from this host's pnpm layout; the allowlist repair completes before that step.

### Failure path

The read was pointed at a real SQLite state whose `channel_pairing_allow_entries` table is missing (proof-only reader override, reverted after the runs):

```console
◇  Doctor warnings
│  Could not read the pairing store for channel signal, account default:  │
│  no such table: channel_pairing_allow_entries. Allowlist sender         │
│  recovery was skipped. Retry openclaw doctor --fix; if it still fails,  │
│  run openclaw doctor to repair the state database.
config sha256 before/after: d0e05286... / d0e05286... (byte-identical; no write)
```

The reviewed head, same command and state, deferred that line to `Doctor changes` and rewrote config (`d0e05286...` -> `3bf182d7...`, only `wizard.lastRunAt`). The intact-state control prints no pairing-store warning.

### Regression (commands shard)

```console
pre-fix (reviewed head): 1 failed | 6 passed (7)
post-fix (candidate):    7 passed (7)
```

Checks: `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` (259 rules, 0 warnings), `git diff --check`, test-lines ratchet (net +7, folded into the existing `it.each`; no new test file, no allocation or baseline change).

prs.title: fix(cli): sanitize channel status diagnostics
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `channels status --probe` writes plugin warning and structured issue text directly into the terminal. An ordinary plugin error can therefore clear the screen, change the terminal title or inject misleading extra lines.

## User Impact

User impact: Human status diagnostics display terminal-safe text with visible newline/carriage-return/tab escapes. JSON retains the original Gateway diagnostic values.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing terminalText helper at the human renderer for both partial warnings and structured issue channel/account/message/fix values. Existing account-row sanitization and renderer-owned separators stay in place.

Related: #193575 independently fixes UTF-16 warning truncation. This patch preserves its separate scope and changes terminal rendering across both diagnostic sections; it does not include that truncation repair.

## Evidence

Product HEAD: `ea5b3cd85995b5f8edc2840db023f611715860ff`; acceptance-red BASE: `eb1a592fc06233963cb8b70ad998f271b8e2da81`.

- **Actual entry:** clean normal QA builds run `node openclaw.mjs channels status --probe --channel report-error --timeout 12000` and the same command with `--json`; ordinary report-normal controls. A normally loaded public-API plugin emits an ordinary status-hook Error and structured diagnostics. The real Gateway executes those hooks and serves channels.status. A transparent recorder forwards the genuine response; no RPC payload is substituted. Actual PTY output and JSON/RPC readback are captured.
- **Same frozen red/green scenario:** BASE human output contains actual clear-screen/color/OSC and bidi controls, plus raw diagnostic line breaks. Exact HEAD removes terminal/format controls and displays data newlines, carriage returns and tabs as visible literals; the raw JSON diagnostic values are preserved.
- **Legal controls and cleanup:** Four cases on both revisions: hostile human/JSON and ordinary human/JSON reports, all exit0. JSON decodes exactly to the actual recorded Gateway response; ordinary reports remain non-partial and issue-free. Configuration bytes stay unchanged, no watchdog fires, and no owned CLI/Gateway/proxy process survives cleanup. The isolated plugin/skill never sends a user message or calls a provider.
- **Checks:** BASE: two intended rendering failures,7 passing controls. HEAD:19 tests across the renderer table and direct command flow pass in 33.317s; existing plain-warning and policy assertions remain. The first cold run timed out in unchanged fallback coverage; the identical command passed after retaining compiler outputs, without assertion or timeout changes. `pnpm test src/commands/channels.surfaces-signal-runtime-errors-channels-status-output.test.ts src/commands/channels.status.command-flow.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. Scoped types, typed lint and formatting pass; clean exact-HEAD QA build 290.720s. Independent GPT-6.1 Sol adversarial review: PASS, no findings.

Reproduce with the [unchanged collector](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/channel-report-proof-v1.py): `python3 channel-report-proof-v1.py CHECKOUT FRESH_OUTPUT NODE26 EXPECTATION channels`. [Environment and observations](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/EVIDENCE.md), [BASE receipt](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/base-receipt.json), [HEAD receipt](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/head-receipt.json), [actual terminal/RPC output](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/head-streams.txt), [independent review](https://github.com/Alix-007/openclaw/blob/57ca9756955750d11161f4ee5ed09dadae3f7bad/independent-review.md).

Production +3/−2 lines; tests +16/−2 lines, 2 files. Existing-solutions preflight: reuse the existing terminalText sanitizer at the human rendering boundary; no new framework, dependency, configuration/default, public protocol/schema, permissions or migration. The complete bounded owner is covered as described above. Upstream CI is checked after publication.

Not tested: Real channel/provider traffic, config-only fallback error rendering, arbitrary event-loop payloads, browser UI, Windows/macOS and production load.

prs.title: fix(cli): surface failed systemd dueling-scope probe in `status --deep`
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw gateway status --deep` on Linux could report a healthy Gateway while the systemd dueling-scope check had never run. When the deep probe threw, `findSystemdGatewayInstallation(serviceEnv).catch(() => null)` turned the failure into `null`, so the result carried neither a warning nor an error: "the probe broke" and "no dueling scope found" printed the same thing. The service-mode startup path in `gateway-cli/run.ts` swallowed the same failure.

- Problem: a failed systemd dueling-scope probe was silently dropped on both paths.
- Solution: keep the redacted probe error on the status payload, print it next to the dueling-scope warning it belongs to, and log it during service-mode startup.
- What changed: `status.gather.ts` records `gateway.duelingScopesWarningError`; `status.print.systemd.ts` renders it; `run-systemd.ts` logs it. The print/inspect code moved into sibling modules to stay inside the line-cap ratchet.
- What did NOT change: a successful probe still prints the existing dueling-scope warning; no new flags, config keys, exit codes, or extra probes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Silence is the wrong default for a diagnostic whose job is to catch a misconfigured host; this is the same silent-swallow class as #195977.

- Best fix: carry the error beside the warning it invalidates, redact at the egress boundary with `redactSupportDiagnosticLine`, and print both from one owner so `status` and startup agree.
- Alternative: rethrow and fail the whole `status` command. Rejected: status is a read-only health report, unrelated checks should still print, and the operator needs the partial result plus a named remedy.
- Risk / non-goals: the probe still only runs on Linux with a native service target (default install identity, no port override, healthy service inspection); this does not widen when it runs.

## User Impact

Operators on Linux now see `Could not inspect the systemd gateway installation: <reason> The dueling-scope diagnosis was NOT checked; run openclaw doctor for the full check.` instead of a silent gap, and the startup log names the same reason and remedy.

## Evidence

Before/after on one machine (Linux, systemd 255, Node 24.19, non-root uid 1000). The failure is real, not mocked: `/etc/systemd/system/openclaw-gateway.service` exists while the system manager does not know it, so the probe throws `ServiceInspectionError: busctl --system call: exit 1; Unit openclaw-gateway.service not loaded.` A real `openclaw gateway run` serves port 18899, then a second real `openclaw gateway run` starts in service mode and evicts it:

| Same scenario, real CLI | Before (`46350da`) | After (this branch) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Startup evicts a stale gateway, probe throws | eviction logged, inspection failure dropped | eviction logged **and** the inspection warning |
| `gatherDaemonStatus` + real printer, probe throws | error undefined, nothing printed | error recorded, warning printed |
| `gateway status --deep`, probe succeeds | no inspection warning | unchanged: no inspection warning |
| `gateway status --deep`, probe fails mid-run | probe access denied, nothing printed | same denied access, warning printed |

```
$ OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER=1 openclaw gateway run --port 18899   # 46350da
[gateway] service-mode: cleared 1 stale gateway pid(s) before bind on port 18899
```

```
$ OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER=1 openclaw gateway run --port 18899   # this branch
[gateway] service-mode: cleared 1 stale gateway pid(s) before bind on port 18899
[gateway] service-mode: could not inspect the systemd gateway installation: busctl --system call: exit 1; Unit openclaw-gateway.service not loaded. busctl --system could not be inspected. The dueling-scope diagnosis was NOT checked; check read access to the reported unit and run openclaw doctor for the full check.
```

Focused tests, same test file, base source vs this branch:

```
# 46350da source, this branch's tests
× surfaces a dueling-scope inspection error when the systemd probe fails
  → expected undefined to be defined
      Tests  1 failed | 1 passed | 53 skipped (55)
```

```
# this branch
✓ reports dueling systemd diagnosis for its native target
✓ surfaces a dueling-scope inspection error when the systemd probe fails
      Test Files  1 passed (1)
           Tests  2 passed | 53 skipped (55)
```

The focused tests above drive the shipped `gatherDaemonStatus` and the shipped `printDaemonStatus`: only the systemd boundary is stubbed, so the collector-to-printer wiring is the real code.

`gateway status --deep` reaches its own probe only after a healthy service inspection, so a mid-run host change is what separates the two failures. Reproduced with the shipped CLI and no stubs: traversal on the user-unit directory was revoked right after the service audit's second `systemctl --user show`, and `strace` shows the deep probe's own discovery call denied 23s later, with no failed inspection in either run.

```
# identical probe syscall, 46350da and this branch
access("[redacted-home]/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service", F_OK) = -1 EACCES
```

```
$ openclaw gateway status --deep      # 46350da
Service: systemd user (enabled)
Runtime: running (pid 280115, state active, sub running, last exit 0, reason 0)
Last shutdown: gateway.stop at 2026-11-10T02:12:06.107Z
```

```
$ openclaw gateway status --deep      # this branch
Service: systemd user (enabled)
Runtime: running (pid 280115, state active, sub running, last exit 0, reason 0)
Last shutdown: gateway.stop at 2026-11-10T02:12:06.107Z
Could not inspect the systemd gateway installation: EACCES: permission denied, access [redacted-path]. The dueling-scope diagnosis was NOT checked; run openclaw doctor for the full check.
```

Per review: use the real daemon-status types instead of a narrow printer type, drop the redundant baseline test, and give the startup warning a recovery step.

prs.title: fix(status): sanitize Gateway-sourced degradation rows before terminal rendering
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw status` (and `openclaw status --all`) renders a "degradation" table via `buildStatusDegradationRows` in `src/commands/status-overview-rows.ts`. Several rows are fed **Gateway-sourced, attacker- or plugin-controlled strings**: `degradedPlugins[].pluginId`, `pluginReload.pluginIds`/`reason`, the `secretEgressProxy` certificate message, and `utilityModelWarnings[].message`. Those values were pushed straight into the terminal table (`rows.push({ Item, Value: decorate(value) })`) **without stripping terminal control sequences**, then printed by the shared `renderTable`. A malicious or buggy Gateway / plugin emitting OSC (`\x1b]0;...\x07`), BEL (`\x07`), or CSI inside those strings can hijack the operator's terminal — set the window title, beep, or inject escapes — merely by an operator running `openclaw status`.

Fix: sanitize every Gateway-sourced degradation value with `sanitizeTerminalText` before it reaches the table, applied as the *inner* operation (`decorate(sanitizeTerminalText(value))`) so theme coloring still wraps the cleaned text.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degradation funnel had **two** raw sinks: the `addWarning` helper (all 7 warning sites) and a bare `rows.push` in the `secretEgressProxy` branch. Both are covered now.

The regression fixture was corrected to use valid `DegradedPlugin` (`state` + `diagnostic`) and `SecretEgressCertificateStatus` (`state: "degraded"` + `caExpiresAt` + `failedCertificates`) records, removing the `as unknown as StatusSummary` laundered cast, and the extracted module-level fixtures are constrained with `satisfies NonNullable<StatusSummary["degradedPlugins"]>[number]` / `satisfies NonNullable<StatusSummary["secretEgressProxy"]>` so discriminants stay literal and the row builder's parameter type checks them directly.

- Source: `src/commands/status-overview-rows.ts` (1 import + 2 call sites).
- Test: `src/commands/status-overview-rows.plugin-reload.test.ts` — typed fixtures, no double assertion; test-line allocation 40 (oxfmt folds the required `state`/`diagnostic`/`caExpiresAt`/`failedCertificates` fields).

## User Impact

Operators running `openclaw status` / `openclaw status --all` are no longer exposed to terminal control-sequence injection from Gateway- or plugin-supplied status strings. Window-title hijacking, beeps, and escape injection via plugin IDs, proxy cert messages, or warning text no longer occur. Normal status text and the trusted warning colour render exactly as before.

## Evidence

### End-to-end proof: shipped CLI reading a live Gateway

A real Gateway was started on a loopback port with an isolated config/state dir, and hostile degradation data was injected into its in-process degraded-plugin registry (`setActiveDegradedPlugins`) **before** it accepted RPC:

```js
pluginId: "bad-npm-pkg\x1b]0;PWNED\x07"   // OSC title + BEL
diagnostic: { kind: "plugin-verification", reason: "missing-install-path",
              detail: "payload\x1b]0;PWNED\x07" }
```

The shipped command then consumed that Gateway over RPC. Gateway `status` reply, hex of `pluginId` (proof the hostile bytes really crossed the wire):

```console
pluginId hex: 6261642d6e706d2d706b67 1b 5d303b50574e4544 07   → ESC ] 0 ; P W N E D BEL
```

Same command, same live Gateway, only `status-overview-rows.ts` swapped (`<ESC>`/`<BEL>` are literal bytes `0x1b`/`0x07`):

| Check | Before (base file) | After (this PR, `e677b3e8`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| command run | `openclaw status` | `openclaw status` |
| Gateway probe | `reachable 5.92s` | `reachable 6.78s` |
| `Degraded plugins` row | `<ESC>[93m1 configured-unavailable · bad-npm-pkg<ESC>]0;PWNED<BEL><ESC>[39m` | `<ESC>[93m1 configured-unavailable · bad-npm-pkg<ESC>[39m` |
| ESC `0x1b` count | 45 | 44 |
| BEL `0x07` count | 1 | 0 |

prs.title: fix(signal): surface rate-limit recovery facts from send failures
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #195280.

When signal-cli rate-limits an outbound message, its JSON-RPC error carries the recovery facts inside `error.data.response.results` — an array of `RATE_LIMIT_FAILURE` entries with `retryAfterSeconds` and, for captcha challenges, a challenge `token`. Both Signal transports only read `error.code` and `error.message`:

- the HTTP transport (client.ts `signalRpcRequest`) surfaced `Signal RPC -5: rate limited, retrying in 12.206 seconds`, dropping the retry window and captcha token entirely;
- the UNIX transport (client.ts `result()`) surfaces the same facts as a bare `Signal RPC -5: remote error` because it intentionally never echoes remote text (PII protection).

Operators had no way to know *when* to retry or that a captcha challenge awaited them, and the challenge token was never reachable from diagnostics.

## What Changed

- Added `SignalRateLimitRecoveryFacts` + `describeSignalRateLimitRecovery(error)`: when `error.code === -5` and `error.data.response.results` contains `RATE_LIMIT_FAILURE` entries, it collects the maximum `retryAfterSeconds` and whether a captcha `token` was present. Nothing personal (recipient identifiers, challenge tokens) enters diagnostics.
- Added `signalRateLimitRecoverySuffix(error)`: renders ` (wait Ns to retry; captcha challenge required; run \`signal-cli submitRateLimitChallenge\` to recover)` only when such facts exist.
- Wired the suffix into both transports' error paths (HTTP `signalRpcRequest` and UNIX `result()`), preserving the existing redaction behavior otherwise.

## Impact

Users on a rate-limited Signal account now see an actionable message with the retry delay and the exact recovery command instead of a dropped or opaque error. Recipient identifiers and challenge tokens stay out of diagnostics (consistent with the existing `quote metadata rejected (redacted)` classification).

## Evidence

- RED: reverting client.ts to `006176e7a91` leaves the 4 new regression tests failing (`4 failed | 42 passed`) — the two transports × (retry window, captcha challenge) cases.
- GREEN: with the fix, the full Signal extension suite passes `492 passed | 3 skipped` across 38 files (2 shards).
- `tsc -p extensions/signal/tsconfig.json --noEmit` exit 0; `oxlint --tsconfig extensions/tsconfig.json` on the 3 changed files 0 warnings 0 errors; `git diff --check` clean.
- New tests live in `extensions/signal/src/client.test.ts` (HTTP) and `extensions/signal/src/client-unix.test.ts` (UNIX), 4 cases each.

### Real shipped-CLI behavior proof (captured terminal output)

Ran the shipped CLI against a stub signal-cli JSON-RPC daemon that rejects the send with signal-cli's real rate-limit payload (`code: -5`, `data.response.results: [{type: "RATE_LIMIT_FAILURE", retryAfterSeconds: 120, token: "..."}]`), configured through the `external-native` transport:

```
openclaw message send --channel signal --target "+15551234567" --message "proof hello"
```

Stub daemon trace (identical on both revisions — the daemon really did reject the send):

```
+67781ms rpc method=send id=1cc1a427-5e92-4b67-a08d-1ea28189fd62
+67781ms reject send with RATE_LIMIT_FAILURE (retryAfterSeconds=120, token present)
```

**Before the fix** (base `2a1330b46dd`) — the recovery facts are dropped:

```
❌ Signal RPC -5: Failed to send message
```

**After the fix** (head `d8cd187bbab`) — retry window and captcha recovery command are surfaced:

```
❌ Signal RPC -5: Failed to send message (wait 120s to retry; captcha challenge required; solve one at https://signalcaptchas.org/challenge/generate.html and run `signal-cli submitRateLimitChallenge --challenge <token> --captcha <result>` to recover)
```

The challenge token itself and the recipient stay out of the diagnostic, which is the redaction contract this change preserves.

## Test Plan

```
OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/signal/src/client.test.ts extensions/signal/src/client-unix.test.ts
```

- 46 passed (including the 8 new rate-limit/captcha cases).
- Full extension: `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/signal` → 492 passed, 3 skipped.

prs.title: fix(cli): show the gateway health reason in status --deep
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw status --deep` prints only `The CLI command failed. For help, run openclaw doctor.` when the Gateway is unreachable, hiding the actual health reason. The reason (`Gateway is unreachable`, or the probe error from a failing health check) was only visible with `--json`.

## User Impact

User impact: `status --deep` now prints the real health reason plus a diagnostic recovery step (`Run openclaw gateway status --deep for gateway diagnostics.`) instead of the generic failure line, with the same exit code 1. The step is a diagnostic command that the service owner never refuses and that applies to local and remote targets alike. `--json` output keeps the stable probe-error message and the exit code is unchanged; no new wording in machine output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The deep status path surfaces a failed gateway health probe by throwing a bare `Error`, which the CLI failure handler classifies as unexpected and replaces with the generic line in human output. Throwing an `ExpectedCliError` instead lets the human output carry the health reason plus a recovery step, matching the actionable-error contract and what the JSON path already reports. The step is deliberately a diagnostic command rather than a lifecycle command: `gateway start`/`gateway install` can be refused by the service owner (for example under an external supervisor), so deriving eligibility from the gateway mode or installation snapshot would recommend commands that are not reliably available. A diagnostic next step needs no such policy and is never refused.

## Evidence

Discriminating regression (`src/commands/status.scan-failure.test.ts`, `status --deep gateway health failures > reports the gateway health reason with a diagnostic recovery step`):

- **BASE** (throw `new Error(health.error)`): both local and remote cases fail — rejection is a plain `Error`, not an `ExpectedCliError`.
- **HEAD** (this change): 8/8 tests in the file pass for both a local and a remote unreachable target.

Real CLI proof through the **supported shipped launcher** (`node openclaw.mjs`, built dist, Node 24, isolated HOME, no Gateway running), same build with only the throw changed:

Before (base):
```
$ openclaw status --deep; echo $?
[openclaw] The CLI command failed.
[openclaw] For help, run `openclaw doctor`.
1
```

After (head):
```
$ openclaw status --deep; echo $?
Gateway is unreachable
Run `openclaw gateway status --deep` for gateway diagnostics.
1
```

`--json` machine output is unchanged (the probe error alone, `{ "ok": false, "error": { "type": "cli_error", "message": "Gateway is unreachable" } }`).

The new first-party audit mock carries a mock-isolation annotation explaining why the real security audit must stay outside this fixture (the deep-status regression only asserts the gateway health failure path).

Test-line budget: 61 added lines, allocated in `config/test-lines-allocations/status-deep-health-reason.txt`.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Scope and alternatives</summary>

This is a narrow single-file change plus its regression test; the TTL-free behavior, JSON schema, and exit codes are unchanged.

Alternatives considered:
- Keeping the bare throw: leaves the health reason hidden in human output.
- Wrapping at the CLI boundary: the `ExpectedCliError` contract already exists for exactly this and is what sibling commands use.
- Human-only recovery text: kept the machine output as the stable probe error so JSON consumers see no wording change.
- Recommending `gateway start`/`gateway install`: rejected because those commands can be refused by the service owner (external supervisor, no installed service), so the hint must not assume either is permitted; a diagnostic command needs no eligibility policy.
</details>

prs.title: fix(channels): surface imessage and whatsapp approval reaction failures on the console
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

iMessage tapback approvals and WhatsApp reaction approvals fail closed when the delivered prompt text no longer correlates with the approval's typed presentation binding — for example when the command itself contains a line that looks like the `ID:` marker. Both plugins correctly return `null`/`false` and disable the reaction path, but they reported the reason through `logging.getChildLogger()`, which writes only to the log file. An operator watching the container console sees reactions silently stop working, with no signal to investigate.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createRuntimeLogging()` in `src/plugins/runtime/runtime-logging.ts` builds plugin child loggers that reach `buildLogger()`, which attaches the file transport and the diagnostic-event transport — never a console sink, because `src/logging/logger.ts` intentionally has no console transport. Both plugins already use `createSubsystemLogger()` elsewhere (`imessage/approvals` in `extensions/imessage/src/approval-handler.runtime.ts`, and `whatsapp/approval-reactions` peers in `approval-handler.runtime.ts`, `inbound/monitor.ts`, `auto-reply/loggers.ts`), so this reuses the existing convention instead of adding a new one.

The change replaces the two file-only child loggers with a module-level subsystem logger per plugin:

- `extensions/imessage/src/approval-reactions.ts`: the binding-correlation mismatch reporter and the resolver `onError` handler share `createSubsystemLogger("imessage/approval-reactions")`.
- `extensions/whatsapp/src/approval-reactions.ts`: the binding-correlation mismatch reporter uses `createSubsystemLogger("whatsapp/approval-reactions")`.

Subsystem `warn` output goes to the console when `consoleLevel` allows it (default `info`), and still reaches the log file, so log-only readers lose nothing. Both call sites stay inside their existing `try`/`catch` guards: logging remains best-effort and cannot mask the replayable resolver failure.

## User Impact

When approval reactions degrade, the container console now carries the reason, for example:

```
approval prompt text failed binding correlation; tapbacks disabled approvalId=exec-... approvalKind=exec
approval prompt text failed binding correlation; reactions disabled approvalId=exec-... approvalKind=exec
approval reaction failed approvalId=... senderId=... error=...
```

The approval still fails closed exactly as before; only its visibility changes.

## Evidence

**RED on base (`origin/main`, 4b077d31b91)** — the new cases fail because the warning never reaches the console:

```
FAIL extensions/whatsapp/src/approval-reactions.test.ts > WhatsApp approval reactions > prints a binding correlation mismatch on the console
AssertionError: expected '' to match /failed binding correlation.*approvalId=exec-console/su
+ Received: ""

FAIL extensions/imessage/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts > iMessage approval reactions > prints a binding correlation mismatch on the console
AssertionError: expected '' to match /failed binding correlation.*approvalId=/su
+ Received: ""
```

**GREEN with the fix:**

```
extensions/imessage/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts  50 passed (50)
extensions/whatsapp/src/approval-reactions.test.ts        22 passed (22)
```

Both cases drive the shipped entry points, set `consoleLevel: "warn"` through `setLoggerOverride`, and assert the console sink gets the line while the return value stays `null`/`false` — the same proof shape as merged #193256.

**Runtime capture** — a real `openclaw gateway run` with the real exec-approval forwarder (isolated state dir, loopback port 19751), replaying one `exec.approval.request` per arm:

![console before and after the fix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SunnyShu0925/openclaw-proof-196051/main/evidence/pr-196051.png)

```
base 4b077d31b91  stderr       (nothing — the fail-closed path stayed invisible)
                  gateway.log  {"plugin":"whatsapp","feature":"approval-reaction-state"} … "reactions disabled"
HEAD c630f1f2     stderr       [whatsapp] approval prompt text failed binding correlation; reactions disabled approvalId=8f1c2d34-…-0000000000aa approvalKind=exec
                               [imessage] approval prompt text failed binding correlation; tapbacks disabled approvalId=8f1c2d34-…-000000000011 approvalKind=exec
                  gateway.log  {"subsystem":"whatsapp/approval-reactions"} and {"subsystem":"imessage/approval-reactions"} — the same two warnings
```

WhatsApp degraded on a prompt whose `warningText` adds an `ID:` line; iMessage degraded when the real 60-char chunker split the prompt so the rejoined visible text no longer contains the reaction hint. Reactions stay disabled in every arm, a healthy prompt in the same run stays silent, and the file log keeps the same records — only the console gate changed. The iMessage `approval reaction failed` (resolver `onError`) line uses that same logger instance and fires when the resolve call itself fails rather than reporting a conflicting decision; binding retention across such an error is asserted in `approval-handler.runtime.test.ts` ("retains the binding on a transient resolver error so a retry can land").

**Checks**

- `node scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts` → `Test lines OK: 6600386; ceiling: 6600386; slack: 0.` (allocation: `config/test-lines-allocations/imessage-whatsapp-approval-reaction-console.txt` = 53)
- `oxlint` on the four changed files → 0 warnings, 0 errors
- `oxfmt --check` on the four changed files → clean
- `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.extensions.json` → no diagnostics in the changed files
- Production net LOC: +9 (four comment lines, two logger owners, otherwise a net reduction on the replaced call chains)

prs.title: fix(nextcloud-talk): surface webhook failure reasons on the container console
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When running `openclaw gateway run` as a daemon or in a container, a Nextcloud Talk webhook failure (e.g. a durable admission failing on a locked SQLite store or disk write) produced no console output at all — the reason went only to the Nextcloud Talk child file log. This PR routes the four webhook log sites through a console-capable subsystem logger so the failure reason appears in container stdout.

- Problem: The `nextcloud-talk` channel's webhook `onError`, the route-conflict warning, the Gateway route-ready note, and the legacy-listener forwarding note all used `core.logging.getChildLogger(...)`, a file-only logger. An operator watching daemon/container logs saw no cause when a webhook admission failed, and the one-time setup guidance for pointing the Nextcloud bot callback at the Gateway port never appeared on stdout.
- Solution: Replace those four log sites with a module-level `createSubsystemLogger("nextcloud-talk/webhook")`, which writes through the subsystem console sink (`console.error`/`console.warn`/`console.log`) while preserving the exact message text and interpolation.
- What changed: `extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.ts` (drop the per-account file-only `logger`, add `webhookLog`, swap the four sites), plus a regression test in `channel.lifecycle.test.ts` asserting the failure reason reaches the console, and a test-lines allocation.
- What did NOT change: no control-flow change; `monitor.ts` and `webhook-spool.ts` untouched (their pre-auth/admission branches still intentionally avoid console noise on unauthenticated floods); the `core` logger-backed runtime helper is retained.

## Why This Change Was Made

Nextcloud Talk is a bundled channel whose webhook failure reasons were observable only in a file log that container/daemon operators often cannot reach. The subsystem logger is the existing console-capable surface the core exposes to extensions (the same one the merged telegram fix `#193256` uses), so this is the minimal, idiomatic route. A child file logger never reaches stdout, where container operators look; errors must name the next step and be visible.

- Best fix: yes — route through `createSubsystemLogger`, matching the already-merged telegram precedent (`c45dd756633`, "media save failures never reach container logs").
- Alternative: adding console output inside `monitor.ts`'s admission catch was rejected — those branches deliberately avoid logging on unauthenticated floods, and the webhook route already returns the real HTTP 500.
- Risk: negligible; message text and interpolation are unchanged, only the sink. The subsystem logger redacts sensitive text and emits to `console.error`/`console.warn`/`console.log` as before.

## User Impact

Operators running `openclaw gateway run` in a daemon/container now see webhook failure reasons (and route-setup notes) on stdout instead of only in an unreachable file log. The first-time setup guidance for pointing the Nextcloud bot callback or reverse-proxy upstream at the Gateway port is now visible where it is needed.

## Evidence

Real end-to-end runtime proof of this PR's `extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.ts` against the shipped `openclaw/plugin-sdk` runtime. No build step: the harness imports the PR's `channel.ts` directly and resolves `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` from the prebuilt Gateway `dist` (the same runtime a container runs).

The harness runs the **real** `nextcloudTalkPlugin.gateway.startAccount` from the PR, which registers the webhook route through the **real** `registerPluginHttpRoute` into a **real** active plugin registry. A real HTTP server dispatches a **real** HMAC-SHA256-signed Nextcloud Talk webhook to the **real** registered handler. The only injected fault is the durable-admission store, stubbed to throw `sqlite unavailable` (the exact operator-visible failure — a locked/unavailable SQLite store), which drives the **real** `onError` → **real** `webhookLog.error` path.

Run command (local paths redacted):

```console
$ node --import tsx proof-harness.mts
```

### Before vs after

Identical harness, identical injected `sqlite unavailable` fault — the only difference is the source file (pre-fix `channel.ts` vs this PR's `channel.ts`):

| Behavior | Before (pre-fix, `core.logging.getChildLogger`) | After (this PR, `createSubsystemLogger("nextcloud-talk/webhook")`) |
|---|---|---|
| Webhook failure reason (`onError`) | written only to the Nextcloud Talk child **file** log — **invisible** to a container/daemon operator | `[nextcloud-talk] [nextcloud-talk:default] webhook error: sqlite unavailable: unable to open database file (ingress admission store)` on **stderr** |
| One-time route-ready note (where to point the bot callback / reverse-proxy upstream) | file-only — **invisible** | `[nextcloud-talk] [nextcloud-talk:default] Gateway webhook route ready at port 18080/nextcloud-talk-webhook; point the Nextcloud bot callback or reverse-proxy upstream here.` on **stdout** |
| Route-conflict warning | file-only | console `warn` |
| Legacy-listener forwarding note | file-only | console `log` |
| Logger implementation | `core.logging.getChildLogger(...)` (file-only sink) | `createSubsystemLogger("nextcloud-talk/webhook")` (console sink: `console.error`/`console.warn`/`console.log`) |
| HTTP status returned to the caller | `500 {"error":"Internal server error"}` | `500 {"error":"Internal server error"}` (unchanged) |
| Control flow / message text | — | unchanged — only the sink changed, not the logic or wording |

### GREEN — PR's fixed `channel.ts` (commit 0fc6a45)

Real captured output (unmodified; ANSI color codes stripped):

```text
[nextcloud-talk] [nextcloud-talk:default] Gateway webhook route ready at port 18080/nextcloud-talk-webhook; point the Nextcloud bot callback or reverse-proxy upstream here.
[nextcloud-talk] [nextcloud-talk:default] webhook error: sqlite unavailable: unable to open database file (ingress admission store)
```

- The `webhook error:` line is the **real** `webhookLog.error(...)` call from `channel.ts`'s `onError` closure, emitted through the real `createSubsystemLogger("nextcloud-talk/webhook")` console sink — not a file-only child logger.
- The route-ready note is the real `startAccount` one-time setup guidance, now on **stdout** where container operators look.

### Real shipped Gateway (`openclaw gateway run`) proof

The harness above is useful integration evidence, but the shipped entry point is
the actual Gateway. This PR's `channel.ts` was exercised through a real
`node openclaw.mjs gateway run` (no build step: the change resolves
`openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` from source via tsconfig paths — the same runtime a
container runs). The `nextcloud-talk` channel was enabled with a bot secret and
base URL; on startup the Gateway registered the webhook route and printed the
one-time setup note on stdout:

```text
[nextcloud-talk] [nextcloud-talk:default] Gateway webhook route ready at port 18765/nextcloud-talk-webhook; point the Nextcloud bot callback or reverse-proxy upstream here.
```

A correctly HMAC-SHA256-signed Nextcloud Talk `Create` webhook (the same
signature scheme the shipped route verifies) is POSTed to that route. The first
request is admitted normally (HTTP 200). The shared state SQLite store
(`state/openclaw.sqlite`, where the durable admission writes) is then locked, and
a second signed webhook is sent — the durable admission
(`channelIngress.enqueueAndClaim`) cannot write, so the Gateway surfaces the
failure on the console while returning HTTP 500:

```console
$ node proof-signed-webhook.mjs
warmup (unlocked) -> HTTP 200            # signed webhook admitted, durably written
locked            -> HTTP 500  body={"error":"Internal server error"}
```

Gateway console (stderr), from the real `openclaw gateway run`:

```text
[nextcloud-talk:default] webhook error: database is locked
[sqlite/transaction] ... operation=channelIngress.enqueueAndClaim ... SQLITE_BUSY (lock-contention) ...
```

The failure reason reaches stdout/stderr via the new subsystem logger and the
HTTP 500 is preserved — the exact shipped behavior this PR fixes. Redacted: base
URL is `https://cloud.example.test`, the bot secret is a local test value, port
`18765`, local PID stripped from the SQLite log line.


### RED — pre-fix `channel.ts` (parent of 0fc6a45, `onError` used `core.logging.getChildLogger`)

Identical harness, identical injected fault, only the source file swapped:

```text
(no `[nextcloud-talk] ... webhook error:` line appears on stdout or stderr)
```

The webhook still returns `500` (admission still fails), but the failure reason is written only to the file-only child logger and is invisible to an operator watching the container console — exactly the gap the table above shows this PR closes.

### Unit regression test

`extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.lifecycle.test.ts` gains a case that drives the real `startAccount` path with `monitor`/`webhook-spool` mocked at the module boundary and asserts the failure reason reaches the console sink via `setLoggerOverride({ level: "silent", consoleLevel: "error", consoleStyle: "compact" })`. It runs in the channels test shard in CI and does not require a live Gateway.

### Open PR collision check

Scanned open PR topics and changed-file lists; no open PR touches `extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.ts`, `monitor.ts`, or `webhook-spool.ts`. The only related open nextcloud-talk PR (#192079) changes `inbound.ts` / `inbound.behavior.test.ts`, which do not overlap.

prs.title: fix(proxy): escape terminal diagnostic values
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw proxy start` and human-readable `proxy validate` output print filesystem paths and diagnostic strings directly. A path or destination containing terminal escapes, line breaks, tabs, or carriage returns can clear or rewrite the displayed diagnostic and add apparent output lines. Ordinary Unicode text is valid data and should remain readable without controlling the terminal.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing `terminalText` formatter at the proxy CLI's human presentation boundary: startup URL/CA/database fields, configuration problems, destination URLs, and both successful/failed check details. Escape values before applying the existing styles. Do not modify the validation owner or its inputs, persistence, JSON diagnostics, raw blobs, or inherited child-process I/O. No custom sanitizer, dependency, configuration, or second output mode is added.

## User Impact

Proxy startup and validation diagnostics retain their own line layout even when a configured path or supplied URL contains controls. Operators can still read ordinary Unicode names and see escaped `\n`, `\t`, and `\r`. Exit codes, recovery guidance, JSON data, and existing proxy-credential redaction remain unchanged. [CLI reference](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/proxy) documents the human/JSON distinction.

## Evidence

Base native build: `b6d8eb287e0898d2c50d89abaef749e4c25ca66a`. Tested source and native build: `5398b23970eb5e239518f00c6f1da314366d42f4`, OpenClaw `2026.11.1`, Linux / Node 24.22.1, November 9, 2026. The subsequently inspected main `5f84a8166dc524a4eab375b16030239acbefc92b` has the same unfixed proxy CLI owner.

### Real CLI RED → GREEN

The same frozen external driver ran the actual built CLI with a private configuration and state directory. Its payload contained `café`, U+001B followed by `[2J`, LF, TAB, and CR. Nothing in the CLI, validation, capture store, or returned output was mocked.

| Actual CLI scenario | Base | Tested head | Independent control/readback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `proxy start --port 0`, controls inside the real state-directory name | CA/DB paths emit raw controls | Paths display `café\nforged\tvalue\rend` without raw controls | Original-path CA file exists; session read back through `proxy sessions --json` |
| `proxy validate`, invalid destination containing the payload | Raw controls in check line | One escaped check line; exit 1 | `--json` retains the original destination and `Invalid allowed destination URL` |
| `proxy validate`, missing CA filename containing the payload | Raw controls in Problems | Escaped error and existing CA recovery guidance; exit 1 | `--json` retains the original error string |

Across all three scenarios, raw-payload observations change from 3/3 on base to 0/3 on head, and escaped-payload observations change from 0/3 to 3/3. An ordinary invalid-destination control still reports the same validation error and exit 1. JSON retains the original diagnostic strings on both revisions.

Actual head output excerpts (`<fixture>` replaces only the temporary directory prefix):

```text
Debug proxy: http://127.0.0.1:43049
CA cert: <fixture>/state café\nforged\tvalue\rend/debug-proxy/certs/root-ca.pem
Capture DB: <fixture>/state café\nforged\tvalue\rend/state/openclaw.sqlite
Press Ctrl+C to stop.

  ✗ allowed invalid:café\nforged\tvalue\rend — Invalid allowed destination URL

proxy sessions --json:
{"sessions":[{"id":"5864d1d9-e33e-4b02-9f1f-79b9b08beaa6",
"mode":"proxy-start","endedAt":1794195993353,...}]}
```

The shown backslash sequences are printable characters in head's human output. The CA file was checked at the original filesystem path containing the actual controls. The native proxy exited cleanly on SIGTERM and its persisted session has a numeric `endedAt`. No private-key bytes were read or printed.

To repeat the validation case from Bash:

```bash
openclaw proxy validate --proxy-url http://127.0.0.1:9 \
  --allowed-url $'invalid:café\e[2J\nforged\tvalue\rend' \
  --denied-url invalid:ordinary
```

Repeat with `--json`: the original destination remains in `checks[0].url`.

Both explicit destinations are invalid, so the validation owner rejects them before any outbound request. The startup listener binds loopback on an ephemeral port; no production state, real channel, model, or external proxy is involved.

<details>
<summary>Focused validation, cost, and limitations</summary>

```sh
node ../replace-four-proxy-proof-20261109.mjs "$PWD" green ../proxy-green.json
```

prs.title: fix(clickclack): print inbound failure warnings on the operator console
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ClickClack inbound turns that fail leave no trace in the gateway console. The worst case: the model returns an empty completion, `handleClickClackInbound` drops the turn, and the user gets no reply while `openclaw gateway run` output stays silent — the only record is a line in the log file. The same gap hides bot-pair loop suppression and agent progress/activity publish failures, all of which only an operator can act on.

## Why This Change Was Made

The handler logged through `runtime.logging.getChildLogger(...)`. That logger is built by `buildLogger()` in `src/logging/logger.ts`, which attaches a single transport — `fileLogTransport.enqueue` — so nothing reaches the console. The console-capable owner is `createSubsystemLogger()` in `src/logging/subsystem.ts`: it writes the same record to the file log and to the console, honoring `logging.consoleLevel`.

This mirrors the owner decision already landed for Telegram media warnings (#193256, `c45dd756633`), which moved the same kind of message off the handler's child logger with the comment "The child file logger never reaches stdout, where container operators look."

Deliberately not changed: the file-level pre-gate in `src/plugins/runtime/runtime-logging.ts` (making every plugin warning console-visible would push all plugin noise to stdout), and the discussion-routing warnings in `extensions/clickclack/src/discussions/*`, which are a separate path and a separate bug.

Message text, control flow, suppression window, and reply delivery are unchanged: the empty-completion branch still returns before any send. The file record keeps the same message and severity, with the binding `{"subsystem":"clickclack/model-reply"}` instead of `{"plugin":"clickclack","feature":"model-reply"}`.

## User Impact

Operators running the gateway in a container or under a service manager now see on the console the four conditions that previously only existed in the log file:

- `[<account>] ClickClack model reply produced no sendable text` — the turn was dropped and no reply was sent
- `[<account>] ClickClack bot-pair loop suppressed for Ns`
- `clickclack progress publish failed: ...`
- `clickclack activity publish failed: ...`

Warn-level console lines go to stderr, which `docker logs`, `journalctl`, and `kubectl logs` collect alongside stdout. No reply content, prefix handling, session routing, or suppression timing changes.

## Evidence

![ClickClack empty-completion warning: operator console vs. log file, before and after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SunnyShu0925/oc-clickclack-proof/main/pr-193951/gateway-console-vs-file-log.png)

Both columns are the captured output of the two isolated runs described below — same ClickClack event, same peer, same empty model completion; only `extensions/clickclack/src/inbound.ts` differs. Text is the captured stderr stream, log file records, and peer request logs, laid out side by side.

Isolated running Gateway on this head, real channel path. `gateway run` uses an isolated state dir; the ClickClack plugin talks to a local server implementing the ClickClack HTTP + realtime contract, which delivers one human DM; the model is a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint returning empty assistant content. Same setup twice: this head, and this checkout with `extensions/clickclack/src/inbound.ts` reverted to `origin/main` (verified byte-identical to main's file).

Operator console (stderr), same event:

```
# base
(no ClickClack line)

# fix
[clickclack] [default] ClickClack model reply produced no sendable text
```

Log file, both runs keep the warning record:

```
# base
{"0":"{\"plugin\":\"clickclack\",\"feature\":\"model-reply\"}","1":"[default] ClickClack model reply produced no sendable text", ...}
# fix
{"0":"{\"subsystem\":\"clickclack/model-reply\"}","1":"[default] ClickClack model reply produced no sendable text", ...}
```

Both runs accepted `message.created` on the realtime WebSocket, re-fetched `GET /api/messages/<id>`, ran one model completion, and sent no reply POST — the turn is still dropped, only its visibility changed.

Handler-level guard in CI: the existing "no sendable text" case in `extensions/clickclack/src/inbound.test.ts` now asserts the console sink. Base source fails that assertion (1 failed | 22 passed); this head passes (23 passed). Four `setup-surface.test.ts` wizard cases fail identically on an unmodified main checkout in this environment (pre-existing, unrelated to this diff); the rest of the suite is untouched by the change.

No live ClickClack workspace was available, so the peer implements the server contract locally; the Gateway ran the shipped adapter, inbound handler, model, and logging owners. Related open PRs: #190322 also edits `extensions/clickclack/src/inbound.ts` (inbound attachments, a different bug); overlap is limited to the import block, so whichever lands second takes a trivial rebase.
