prs.title: fix(channels): preserve enabled state on partial channel updates
prs.body:
## Description

Partial channel updates used to re-validate only the fields in the request, so every omitted field was reset to its schema default — a credentials-only re-save silently turned `enabled` off and the channel stopped receiving messages with no warning.

This merges the saved channel config under the incoming fields before validation, so omitted fields keep their saved values and only explicitly sent values change anything. A genuinely new channel still gets schema defaults. Saving now logs a warning when a channel's enabled state actually flips, startup warns about a configured-but-disabled channel, and rebuilding a missing agent.json from the stale root copy warns instead of silently switching channels off.

Note: the rebuild case only warns — the rebuilt profile still takes the root values, since the root copy is frozen at migration time and never synced from agent.json. Fixing that sync is separate work.

## What Problem This Solves

Issue #8475: a partial channel re-save silently reset `enabled` to its schema default (`false` for QQ), so the channel stopped receiving messages with no warning and no visible change. The same hole affected every channel: any omitted persisted field was re-defaulted on every partial update. With merge-before-validation, omitted fields keep their saved values, and an actual enabled flip is logged.

## Evidence

Reproduce-first check (repro cases now in `tests/unit/app/routers/test_config_router.py` and `tests/unit/config/test_config_model_validators_and_legacy_migration.py`):

- Before the fix: the original repro failed 3/3 on pristine HEAD `2cf28d14` (partial PUT re-defaulted `enabled`, bulk PUT re-defaulted `enabled`, rebuild from the stale root copy silently disabled the channel).
- After the fix: the adapted repro passes 3/3 (partial + bulk PUT preserve `enabled`; the rebuild case logs the warning through the real `load_agent_config` path).

Focused suites (with the fix): 193 passed, 17 skipped (`test_config_router`, validators/migration, agent-config-persistence, channel-shape-consistency) — baseline was 182 passed; the +11 are the new tests (merge-boundary unit test, partial/bulk PUT preservation, explicit-disable + warning log, no-warning-when-no-flip, new-channel schema defaults, Discord genericity, explicit-`""` clears a value, rebuild warning, silence for unconfigured channels, helper default-comparison).

Full suite: 321 failures were recorded, none in any changed or adjacent file. A `git stash` re-run of exactly those 321 on pristine main reproduces 316 identically (pre-existing); 4 more are timing-sensitive flakes that pass on re-run. One failure could not be pinpointed after a VM restart wiped the saved failure list.

Pre-commit: a scoped `run --all-files` over the 7 changed files passes every hook (mypy, black, flake8, pylint + file hooks). The full-repo verdict was lost when the runtime restarted mid-run.

Fixes #8475

Disclosure: AI coding assistance was used in preparing this change.

prs.title: feat(providers): add model fallback metadata to chat response
prs.body:
## Description

When the daemon silently switches models mid-request, nothing in the response says which model actually answered. This adds four fields to the chat response metadata and to the fallback event, so the switch is visible:

- `model_used` — the model that served the response
- `model_requested` — the model the user asked for (the primary)
- `fallback_reason` — why the switch happened, e.g. `transient (503)`
- `fallback_chain_position` — zero-based position of the serving model in the chain (0 = primary, 1 = first fallback)

The reason is built from the classified error kind plus the HTTP status only — raw provider error text is never used, since it can contain API keys or tokens. The existing `qwenpaw_model_fallbacks` and `qwenpaw_actual_model` keys are untouched, and the new event fields are additive for Console/channel consumers (they only read the existing fields).

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8103

Note: 401/403 errors still do not trigger a fallback — that is deliberate policy (see `test_does_not_fallback_on_authentication_error`), so the issue's literal 401 example does not fall back at HEAD. The tests exercise the same gap with 503s.

## What Problem This Solves

Issue #8103: a silent model fallback is invisible to the user — the daemon serves the answer from a different model without saying so. With these fields, the response itself (and the fallback event that reaches the Console and channels) names the requested model, the model that actually served, why it switched, and where that model sits in the chain.

## Evidence

Reproduce-first check (repro cases now in `tests/unit/providers/test_fallback_chat_model.py`):

- Before the fix: 2 failed (`KeyError: 'model_used'` on the final non-streaming response and on the last streaming chunk), 1 passed (401 control — no fallback, by policy).
- After the fix: 3/3 pass.

Focused suites (with the fix):

```
40 passed in 2.16s
```

(`tests/unit/providers/test_fallback_chat_model.py` + `tests/unit/agents/test_reasoning_fallback_bridge.py` — 32 baseline tests plus 8 new tests: non-streaming, streaming last chunk, structured output, multi-hop position, secret-leak, metadata preservation, no-fallback control, sink event fields.)

Full unit suite: 16,564 passed with this change. The failures present (172 failed, 57 errors) match pristine `main` (170 failed, 57 errors, identical error set); the 3 differing failures are load-dependent flakes that pass in isolation on both trees. `pre-commit run --all-files` passes.

Disclosure: AI coding assistance was used in preparing this change.

issues.body:
### Problem

`StoragePolicy::Rolling` (the default storage policy for all unconfigured instances — `crates/zeroclaw-log/src/config.rs:46`, `default_log_persistence()` in `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:11545-11547`) has a serious performance regression under sustained event volume.

After every event write, `trim_to_last_entries` (`crates/zeroclaw-log/src/writer.rs:635-700`) checks whether the active file's line count exceeds `max_entries`. There is no hysteresis: once over the cap, the trim runs on essentially every subsequent write. Each trim does two full linear scans of the active file (one pass via `count_nonempty_lines` to count lines, one pass to copy the retained lines into a temp file), then an atomic rename. Once the active file grows large, this becomes an O(file size) operation per event.

This creates a self-sustaining deadlock during config reload: `init_from_config` must drain the write queue and wait for the old worker thread to exit before installing a new policy (`shutdown_current_writer`, `writer.rs:223-276`). If the write worker is busy doing a multi-hundred-MB full-file rewrite on every event, the write queue never drains fast enough, so reload hangs or times out — including reloads meant to switch *away* from `rolling` to a less expensive policy.

A visible side effect: any error mid-trim, or the process being killed before the final `rename`, leaves an orphaned `runtime-trace.tmp.<pid>.<nanosecond-timestamp>` file behind. There is no cleanup path for these on error, on kill, or on startup — they accumulate indefinitely. Observed in the wild: dozens of orphaned tmp files ranging from ~24MB to ~190MB, spanning several days, all named identically to what `trim_to_last_entries` produces at `writer.rs:643-647`, alongside a runtime-trace.jsonl that had grown to 208MB (driven further by `log_tool_io = "full"` / `log_llm_request_payload = "full"`, which skip truncation entirely).

More fundamentally: for a "keep the most recent N entries" semantic, the standard implementation pattern (used by systemd-journald, Kafka log segments, logrotate) is to make eviction cost independent of total retained size — evict whole segments, never rewrite the retained portion. `Rolling`'s literal single-file implementation does the opposite.

### Proposal

Retire `StoragePolicy::Rolling` in three phases, folding its semantics into `Rotating`.

**Phase 1 — add an entry-count rotation trigger to `Rotating`**

Add a new `[observability]` field (working name `log_persistence_max_entries_per_segment`) so `Rotating` can rotate when the active file reaches N lines, alongside the existing `log_persistence_max_bytes` and `log_persistence_rotate_daily` triggers. Rotation is the existing O(1) whole-file rename to an archive name (`rotate_active`, `writer.rs:769-783`); no content is rewritten. `run_retention` prunes old archives by count/age as it already does.

**Phase 2 — extend the query layer to read across segment files**

`GET /api/logs` (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_logs.rs`) currently opens the single path returned by `runtime_trace_path()`. Change the read path to enumerate all non-expired archive files plus the active file, in order, and present them as one merged logical event stream for pagination. Extend the pagination cursor (currently a byte offset, `next_cursor_line_offset`) to a composite that also identifies which segment file it points into. For a deployment configured with only entry-count rotation and small segments, this query semantics is equivalent to today's `Rolling`: callers still see a complete "most recent N events" window, just assembled from multiple files instead of one.

**Phase 3 — deprecate and remove `StoragePolicy::Rolling`**

Once Phase 1+2 are stable, mark `log_persistence = "rolling"` deprecated, then remove the enum variant and `trim_to_last_entries` in a subsequent minor release. The orphaned-tmp-file problem disappears as a side effect since nothing produces that file pattern anymore.

### Design sketch

Affected surfaces:
- `crates/zeroclaw-log/src/writer.rs` — add `maybe_rotate_for_entry_count`; eventually remove `trim_to_last_entries`
- `crates/zeroclaw-log/src/config.rs` — new config field; update `StoragePolicy`/`ResolvedPolicy`
- `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs` — mirror the new `ObservabilityConfig` field; adjust defaults
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_logs.rs` — multi-segment enumeration + merged read; extended cursor shape
- `docs/book/src/` — observability/log-persistence docs

Proposed phases: Phase 1 and Phase 2 can ship in the same PR (the new rotation trigger is only useful once the query layer can read across segments). Phase 3 should be a separate PR for easier rollback/audit.

### Alternatives considered

1. **Add hysteresis to `trim_to_last_entries` (a stopgap patch)**: change the trigger to `max_entries * 1.2` and trim down to `max_entries * 0.8`. This amortizes the full-file rewrite roughly 5x but the underlying O(file size) cost per triggered trim is unchanged — large files still degrade linearly, and the orphaned-tmp-file problem remains unresolved. Could land as an interim patch ahead of Phase 1.
2. **`fallocate(FALLOC_FL_COLLAPSE_RANGE)`**: a Linux-specific primitive that can remove a byte range from the start of a file without copying the retained content. Requires both offset and length to be filesystem-block-size multiples (typically 4096 bytes), which does not naturally align with variable-length JSONL line boundaries — using it safely would require either accepting "approximately N" retention or padding writes to force block alignment. It is also ext4/xfs-only on Linux, with no equivalent on macOS/Windows, which is a problem for the project's cross-platform (Tauri) desktop targets.
3. **Keep `Rolling`, just patch orphan cleanup + hysteresis**: treats the symptom, not the redundancy — leaves a policy whose semantics are already a strict subset of what `Rotating` + entry-count rotation would provide, at higher long-term maintenance cost.

### Non-goals

- No change to the JSONL line-level format.
- Phase 2's multi-segment query does not require special optimization for full-text `q=` search across archives — the existing per-line filter logic can scan sequentially across segments; result-set size is bounded by `retention_max_files`.
- No binary log format or external storage backend in this RFC.

### Risks and mitigations

**Existing-config compatibility**: instances with `log_persistence = "rolling"` + `log_persistence_max_entries = N` in their config must keep working through Phase 1/2. When Phase 1 lands, the config loader should transparently map `rolling` to `rotating` + `log_persistence_max_entries_per_segment = N` at runtime, emitting a one-line deprecation warning at startup. Only in Phase 3 should `rolling` actually fail to parse, and that change needs to be called out prominently in the CHANGELOG and a migration note.

**`/api/logs` cursor format change**: the extended cursor is a forward-compatible additive change; old byte-offset-only cursors can still be interpreted as "resume from this offset in the active file." Callers still using the already-`#[deprecated]` `next_cursor` field (`api_logs.rs:37-43`, deprecated since 0.8.0) are unaffected.

**Default value change**: today's default is `Rolling` + `max_entries = 200`. Post-Phase-3, the default needs to move to `Rotating` with a sensible default (e.g. `log_persistence_max_bytes` ~10MB or `log_persistence_max_entries_per_segment` ~1000, plus `retention_max_files = 5`). That default should be confirmed separately once Phase 2 is done and the Phase 3 removal PR is drafted.

### Breaking change?

Yes - existing configurations, APIs, or defaults change

### Decision and revisit surface

This issue is the design-discussion entry point. The Phase 1 patch PR should link back here. The Phase 3 removal PR needs to re-confirm the chosen defaults in its PR description before merge.

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.

issues.title: [Bug]: runtime-trace.jsonl loses hours of events across daemon restarts (handoff buffer / queue drops / silent writer)
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`runtime-trace.jsonl` shows multi-hour coverage gaps on a busy daemon even though agent work provably continued during the gap. On our production instance (Windows service, 0.8.7) the trace covers 2026-11-09 18:43–18:46 UTC, then one rotated file with **zero** events, then nothing until 2026-11-10 22:27 UTC — while the agent workspaces show files written by agent runs at 2026-11-09 22:34 and 2026-11-10 15:00 local (those runs necessarily made LLM calls and tool calls, all of which should have produced trace events).

Rotation is 200 entries per file, and the persistence worker already `sync_all`s every 1 s / 100 writes, so a hours-long hole cannot be explained by the steady-state durability window. The gap aligns with a restart-heavy period, which points at events never reaching the file:

1. The in-process handoff buffer (used to replay events into the next file on writer re-init) is lost when the process is killed before a re-init happens.
2. Events can be dropped on the full 1024-entry queue (`try_send` failure drops with only a `tracing::warn!`).
3. After a config reload or restart sequence, the serving instance may run with the trace writer not installed or with a dead worker, silently producing nothing.

### Expected behavior

Every processed turn leaves durable trace events. A daemon restart (graceful or forced) must not erase coverage: pending events should be flushed/drained on shutdown, and a writer that is not installed or dead should be loud, not silent.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the daemon as a Windows service with trace persistence enabled and a busy Telegram channel.
2. Restart the service several times over a day (`Restart-Service -Force` / `Stop-Service -Force` + start), including during active agent sessions.
3. Compare `data/state/runtime-trace*` coverage against workspace file mtimes: agent-written workspace files appear inside trace gaps.

### Impact

Affected users: anyone relying on `runtime-trace.jsonl` for cost/quota accounting or incident review.
Frequency: intermittent, correlates with restarts.
Consequence: usage analytics and incident timelines silently under-report; we lost a full day of per-agent token accounting (the missing window is exactly when a heavy user session ran).

### ZeroClaw version

0.8.7 (v0.8.7-176-g1c003efff0)

### Operating system

Windows 11 (service-managed daemon)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

---

**We can contribute the fix.** Our current thinking: drain/flush the log writer from the daemon's shutdown path (the `WriterJob::Shutdown` machinery in `zeroclaw-log` already exists but is only invoked on writer re-init, not on process/service stop), persist or eagerly flush the handoff buffer instead of holding it in-process, and emit a loud warning when the queue drops events or the worker is dead. Happy to take this on if the approach sounds right.

issues.title: [Feature]: Write-only WebUI credential management and scoped secret references
issues.body:
### Summary

Provide an operator-only credential catalog under Storage → Secrets: metadata-only listing, write-only creation/replacement, disable/delete actions, and controlled credential references for approved tasks. Draft PR #12402 covers write-only management for existing plugin TLS bindings. This issue tracks the broader catalog and scoped runtime references.

### Problem statement

Operators need to provision service credentials without pasting them into agent conversations, model prompts, session history, or skills. Existing encrypted configuration and masked secret fields provide useful building blocks, but configuring a credential is different from authorizing an agent/tool to use it.

An operator should be able to say “query the service using credential `monitoring-api`”; the model should handle a reference, while an authorized backend component supplies authentication.

The security objective is to let agents perform explicitly authorized operations without exposing passwords, API tokens, private keys, or other secret values to the model. The agent supplies an alias. A trusted consumer enforces the grant and applies authentication inside its execution boundary. With an external vault such as OpenBao, ZeroClaw persists the reference and grant metadata while the secret value remains in the vault and is fetched at use time. This reduces what can be recovered from the host's persistent storage or backups. A compromised running daemon, service identity, or unrestricted process with the same privileges may still be able to request secrets within that identity's vault policy.

### Proposed solution

**1. Administrative UI**

- List only identifier, type, configured/disabled state, permitted consumers/destinations, and appropriate lifecycle metadata.
- Create or replace a secret through a password/multiline draft field over the authenticated administrative API.
- Once saved, return only set/not-set state or a fixed mask. No reveal, copy, export, plaintext read endpoint, or value-length disclosure.
- Support explicit disable and delete, with dependency warnings and clear confirmation. Explain that deletion from ZeroClaw does not revoke a credential at its upstream service or erase existing backups.
- Keep the submitted draft transient; clear it after success, cancellation, and navigation. Do not persist it in browser storage, conversation state, analytics, or error reports.

**2. Controlled use by reference**

- Expose an identifier to the model, never a generic tool that returns the stored value.
- Resolve the reference within the existing trusted tool/connector execution boundary. Reuse applicable plugin secret-binding mechanisms rather than creating a second source of policy.
- Bind use to explicitly authorized agents/components and, where applicable, trusted destinations and operations. Possession of a reference must not grant permission.
- Preserve tool approvals, sandboxing, destination policy, and normal operation authorization. A chat instruction may request use but cannot create a credential grant.
- Re-evaluate current authorization and credential enabled/version state at use time; do not retain stale grants after disable, replacement, or permission revocation.
- Ensure authentication is not forwarded on cross-origin redirects or to model-selected arbitrary endpoints. Do not interpolate secret values into arbitrary shell text, URLs, or process command lines.

**3. Storage and API protections**

- Reuse the established SecretStore/key-source abstraction and an appropriate canonical storage owner; do not introduce custom cryptography or a parallel plaintext store.
- This feature must refuse secret writes if encrypted storage is unavailable/disabled; it must not silently inherit plaintext storage.
- List metadata without decrypting values. Credential value writes and lifecycle mutations remain operator-only, including authorization revalidation at commit time.
- Apply the established session/origin/CSRF protections, no-store responses, input bounds, and safe error handling.
- Audit actor, credential identifier, consumer, operation and outcome, never the value. Secret values must not enter prompts, memory, tool results, receipts, logs, telemetry, or traces.

### Example operator workflow

1. Open **Config → Storage → Secrets**, choose **Add credential**, and enter a reference name such as `MEU_GMAIL`. Choose the credential type and supply its value in the write-only form. For OAuth, complete the provider's consent flow with the requested scopes.
2. Bind that reference to an approved agent and connector, with explicit destinations and operations where applicable. For `MEU_GMAIL`, grant a Gmail connector read-only access to the authorized mailbox.
3. In chat, ask “Read my unread Gmail messages using `MEU_GMAIL`.” The model sends the reference and operation to the connector. The backend checks the current grant, uses OAuth to read the mailbox and returns the authorized results. Chat and tool output contain no OAuth tokens.
4. Return to Secrets to replace, disable, re-enable, or delete the credential. The list shows metadata and state. A disabled reference denies subsequent use.

| Credential type | What the operator provisions | Example request by reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TLS certificates and keys | PEM CA certificate, client certificate and private key, or a supported certificate file format such as CER/DER | “Check the inventory API using `INVENTORY_MTLS`.” The connector uses the configured TLS profile for the approved destination. |
| API token or key | A token in a write-only field | “List open findings using `SCANNER_API`.” The scanner connector authenticates to its configured origin. |
| Username and password | A credential record containing a username and write-only password | “Check the account status using `PORTAL_LOGIN`.” An approved connector performs authentication for the configured service. |
| TOTP | A write-only enrollment seed bound to an approved authentication flow | “Run the approved status check using `OPS_MFA`.” The connector generates the one-time code in the backend and supplies it only to that service's authentication flow. |
| OAuth | Consent for an approved connector and its requested scopes | “Read my unread Gmail messages using `MEU_GMAIL`.” The Gmail connector uses the mailbox's read-only grant. |
| Other connector-specific secrets | For example, an SSH private key bound to an approved SSH connector | “Check uptime on the approved host using `FLEET_SSH`.” The SSH connector authenticates within its existing host and operation policy. |

These examples describe the target behavior. Each credential type needs a compatible consumer with explicit policy. The identifier alone grants no access. Secrets, derived TOTP codes and authentication headers stay inside the trusted execution boundary.

### External secret providers

Under **Config → Storage → Secrets**, show each registered credential's source alongside its alias and configured/disabled state. Example sources are **Local encrypted storage**, **1Password**, and **OpenBao**. An operator can bind an existing external reference to an alias such as `SCANNER_API` without copying the secret into local storage. In chat, “List open findings using `SCANNER_API`” works through the same consumer and destination grants regardless of the source.

- **1Password.** Reuse ZeroClaw's existing `op://` reference integration. Show the provider and binding state, and let authenticated operators configure references such as `op://Operations/Scanner/token`. Use the existing backend integration and a least-privilege service identity.
- **OpenBao.** Propose a KV v2 backend with an operator-configured server profile and an explicit mount, path, and field, for example mount `kv`, path `integrations/scanner`, field `token`. Keep authentication server-side, verify TLS, and restrict the service identity to the required paths.
- **Additional providers.** The same backend interface could support Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Cloud Secret Manager, and other secret managers. Each adapter would use native provider authentication and least-privilege policies, with the same alias, binding state, and consumer authorization in ZeroClaw.
- List only references registered in ZeroClaw and their metadata. Keep external locators operator-only. Resolve values within the approved backend consumer and fail closed on denied or unavailable references. List operations must not fetch secret values.
- Start with binding and unbinding existing external secrets. Disabling or deleting a ZeroClaw binding affects local use. Rotation and deletion in the external vault remain under that provider's policies. Evaluate external write support separately.

References: [1Password secret references](https://www.1password.dev/cli/secret-references) and [OpenBao KV v2](https://openbao.org/docs/secrets/kv/kv-v2/).

### Credential usage grants and SSH-first rollout

Add **Usage permissions** under Secrets, with a credential-centered view and links from each consumer profile. One alias can have multiple independent grants. Each grant identifies the consumer type and instance, permitted agent where applicable, exact destination and compatible authentication slot. The backend enforces these grants alongside existing tool approvals and operation policy. Keep grants default-closed, check live authorization before each use, and audit alias, consumer, destination and outcome.

1. **SSH keys first.** Add an **SSH keys** tab with alias, source, configured state, public-key fingerprint when available, and authorized destinations. Support write-only private-key provisioning through local encryption or external references. An SSH grant binds host, port and remote user and requires verified server host keys. Resolve the key inside the SSH executor or its agent and keep it out of model context and command arguments. Preserve task-owned connection reuse, close on task termination and enforce an idle limit. Include credential/grant identity in connection reuse and make revocation effective before the next command on an existing connection. Test a key authorized on two hosts, refused on a third, then revoked for one while the other still works.
2. **HTTP and MCP.** Preserve existing HTTP aliases and exact HTTPS origin rules. Remote MCP grants bind the configured server instance, origin and authentication field. Local MCP delivery requires a separate explicit grant and a documented trusted process boundary because that process receives the value. Re-evaluate grants before reuse of any authenticated connection.
3. **Plugins and skills.** Reuse plugin TLS profiles for host-applied client identities. Any plugin access to a raw value requires an explicit capability and instance grant. Skills, SOPs and scheduled work can declare alias requirements and call authorized consumers. Their declarations confer no access. Arbitrary Bash or Python injection is outside the initial scope.

A grant authorizes authentication and does not authorize arbitrary operations. Keep provider identities and transport verification under operator control. Treat this as a proposed extension of #12408, with SSH as the first implementation slice, and seek maintainer feedback on ownership before expanding the runtime boundary.


### Non-goals / out of scope

- A general password manager with stored-value retrieval or export.
- A new master-key algorithm, universal vault replacement, automatic import of existing secrets, or a new MITM proxy.
- An unrestricted shell secret-injection tool.
- Claiming that encryption at rest or a write-only UI isolates secrets from a compromised daemon or unrestricted same-user shell. That requires a separately assessed execution/security boundary.
- Automatically migrating, revoking upstream credentials, or changing existing installations' behavior.

### Alternatives considered

- Continue provisioning through CLI/configuration: useful, but lacks the requested administrative workflow.
- Supply secrets through chat/skills: creates avoidable exposure and should not be the intended provisioning path.
- External secret managers: retain them as a possible backend direction rather than requiring every installation to run an additional service.

Related: #12001 (broader egress proxy and secret substitution), #8398 (plugin permissions/config/secrets model), #8556 (set/not-set secret UI), and #12142 (existing public discussion of daemon-state access). This proposal should complement their ownership and threat-model decisions, not duplicate or bypass them.

### Acceptance criteria

- Network responses and metadata listing never disclose saved values or lengths.
- Unauthorized, revoked, cross-agent and wrong-destination use is denied, including authorization changes between request admission and commit/use.
- Create/replace/disable/delete are covered through the real API and UI boundaries; duplicate identifiers, concurrent changes, missing key material and storage failure have explicit behavior.
- Regression tests verify no secret appears in model input, output, history, audit payloads or error responses.
- Existing consumers/configuration remain compatible. Stored ciphertext and metadata have one canonical owner; no new long-lived policy snapshot becomes authoritative.

### Architecture impact

Gateway administration, dashboard Storage UI, encrypted secret storage, and narrowly scoped tool/connector credential resolution. Reuse existing ownership, authentication and permission contracts. The administrative UI and runtime reference consumption can be separate PRs after the design is agreed.

Please advise which existing subsystem should own the catalog, whether reference consumption should be planned under #12001/#8398, and whether the eventual design crosses the RFC trigger for a material security-model change or a new subsystem. This issue does not assume that approval.

### Risk and rollback

Principal risks are credential disclosure, confused-deputy use, stale authorization, and a misleading isolation promise. Keep the capability opt-in and default closed, enforce grants server-side, document limits, and preserve encrypted-state backups. Disabling the new surface should leave existing credential consumers unchanged; any migration needs a separately reviewed rollback plan.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment.

### Next decision surface

Discussion on this issue and the related security/plugin design trackers. Seek maintainer feedback on ownership and authorization for the remaining scope. Promote to an RFC if the substantive design requires it.

### Breaking change?

No intended breaking change.

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] Removed personal/sensitive data and deployment-specific details.
- [x] Used neutral, project-focused identifiers and examples.

### SSH key custody and transport lifetime

The operator registers a write-only OpenSSH key or an external reference and explicit host, port, and remote-user grants. For OpenBao, the daemon persists the encrypted reference, fetches the key under its narrowly scoped service identity, and passes it over stdin to an ephemeral OpenSSH agent. The helper does not create a private-key file or expose the value to the model, command arguments, or tool output. The signer socket is under a mode-0700 task directory owned by the service user, and agent forwarding is disabled. The broker requires strict server host-key verification.

Once OpenSSH creates its authenticated multiplex listener, the broker shuts down the signer and unlinks its socket before granting the first command. Later commands reuse the authenticated connection and recheck the current destination grant. A revoked grant blocks subsequent broker commands even if a transport already exists. The master itself is closed on task completion, cancellation, or idle expiry.

The service account and root remain trusted. A process with the same UID may reach the signing socket during authentication or the authenticated multiplex socket during the task. Per-destination grants are enforced by the broker. Host isolation and least-privilege vault policy bound the impact of same-UID compromise. This design does not claim a security boundary against a compromised daemon or unrestricted same-UID execution.

## Service credentials and authenticated callers

The operator owns the backend, service credentials and grants. An authorized user invokes a bounded operation without access to the credential value. Trusted caller identity is useful for authorization and audit even when users share one downstream service identity. Personal delegation stays with a separate user-controlled flow and contract. See #12422 for the detailed design and #12441 for trusted caller identity.

issues.title: [Bug]: gateway logs every connection at INFO through spawn!, flooding the runtime trace
issues.body:
### Affected component

gateway/api

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

Since #11901, the gateway runs every accepted connection through `ServeTasks::spawn`, and `ServeTasks` is also hyper's executor. `ServeTasks::spawn` goes through `zeroclaw_spawn::spawn!` (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1079` on master `3a3f2e3586`), and that macro records a `task spawned` and a `task complete` event at INFO for every task.

So every HTTP connection to the gateway now writes two INFO records to the runtime trace. A client that doesn't reuse connections (a reverse proxy that opens a new upstream connection per request, or a dashboard polling a few endpoints) turns into a steady flood. On one install, a web UI polling through a proxy opened about 6.5 connections a second. That's about 13 trace records a second, all from `lib.rs:1079`, and they push out everything else.

### Expected behavior

Per-connection serve tasks, and the tasks hyper hands to the executor, shouldn't produce INFO records. They are routine and high-volume. Possible fixes (maintainers' call):

- record these sites at DEBUG or TRACE, for example with a quiet variant of `spawn!` used by `ServeTasks`;
- or make the `spawn!` lifecycle records DEBUG by default and keep INFO for the long-lived tasks where the spawn/complete pair is useful.

Connection-level events that matter (errors, admission refusals after a stop) should still be recorded.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Run a daemon with trace persistence on (the default "rolling" policy is enough)
zeroclaw daemon

# 2. Make plain HTTP requests without connection reuse
for i in $(seq 1 200); do curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:42617/health; done

# 3. Count spawn-lifecycle records by site in the runtime trace
#    (default log_persistence_path; adjust for another config dir)
python3 - <<'EOF'
import collections, json, pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("~/.zeroclaw/data/state/runtime-trace.jsonl").expanduser()
c = collections.Counter()
for line in p.open():
    a = json.loads(line).get("attributes") or {}
    if "task_site" in a:
        c[a["task_site"]] += 1
print(c.most_common(3))
EOF
# Observed on the v0.9.0 release binary with a fresh, empty config dir:
#   100 INFO task spawned crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1079
#   100 INFO task complete crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1079
# The trace held exactly 200 lines, all of them these records: the default rolling
# window is 200 entries, so the daemon's own startup events were already gone.
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone with trace persistence on and a gateway client that opens short connections (proxies, dashboards, health checks).
Frequency: always, in proportion to the connection rate.
Consequence:
- The trace's history window collapses. With `rotating`, 16 MiB segments and 14 kept files, one install went from about two weeks of history to about 7 hours (a new segment every ~30 minutes). With the default `rolling` policy (`log_persistence_max_entries = 200`), 100 HTTP requests replace the whole trace; at that install's rate that is about 15 seconds of history.
- Real events (turn errors, memory warnings) are evicted before anyone reads them, which hurts incident forensics.
- Steady disk writes (about 0.75 GB/day in that case), which matters on SD-card hosts such as a Raspberry Pi.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
# spawn-lifecycle records per task_site, counted per trace segment

# v0.8.6-based build (before #11901):
span 2026-11-12T07:57:17.770Z -> 2026-11-12T10:53:13.301Z events 890
      109 task spawned   crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/openai_codex.rs:1644
      109 task complete  crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/openai_codex.rs:1644
       25 task spawned   crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs:2338
       25 task complete  crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs:2338

# v0.9.0-based build, same install and clients:
span 2026-11-15T09:27:05.863Z -> 2026-11-15T10:00:45.740Z events 36194
    18097 task complete  crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1079
    18097 task spawned   crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1079
```

### ZeroClaw version

Reproduced on the v0.9.0 release binary (`zeroclaw 0.9.0 (6c78ba5)`, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu). First seen on v0.9.0-93 (upstream `87461d1ac5` plus a few unmerged PRs that don't touch `zeroclaw-spawn`, `zeroclaw-log` or `ServeTasks`). The code path is unchanged on master `3a3f2e3586`

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)

### Operating system

Fedora-based Linux x86_64 (release-binary reproduction); Debian-based Linux aarch64 on a Raspberry Pi (where it was first seen)

### Regression?

Yes, it worked before

### Pre-flight checks

- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: cost.enforcement.mode is ignored, so an exceeded budget always stops the turn, even in the default "warn" mode
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S1 - workflow blocked

### Current behavior

`[cost.enforcement] mode` is parsed (default `"warn"`), but nothing in the runtime reads it. Once a model is priced and a projected daily or monthly total passes `daily_limit_usd` / `monthly_limit_usd`, `enforce_tool_loop_budget` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/provider_call.rs`, master `3a3f2e3586`) always ends the turn with `TurnStop::fatal(TurnStopCode::BudgetExhausted, …)`, whatever the mode. Every later turn is refused until the period resets.

Gateway chat turns run inside the same budget scope (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs`), so a dashboard user is cut off too.

With the defaults (`daily_limit_usd = 10.0`, `monthly_limit_usd = 100.0`, `mode = "warn"`), adding a rate sheet so that cost tracking works is enough to stop an agent mid-task on its first heavy day. Before rates are added the limits never trigger, because unpriced tokens record $0.

Related #11585, which covers `allow_override` and limits that don't refresh after an RPC config change. This report is the separate case of the mode itself.

### Expected behavior

As `docs/book/src/ops/cost-tracking.md` describes:

- `warn` (the default): record the event with a warn-level log and let the request through;
- `block`: refuse the request with a `BudgetExceeded` error;
- `route_down`: substitute `route_down_model`.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Run against the v0.9.0 release binary, with a local mock of an OpenAI-compatible
# endpoint that answers every chat request with usage.prompt_tokens = 10000.

# config.toml (throwaway config dir):
#   schema_version = 4
#   [providers.models.openai.mock]
#   model = "mock-model"
#   uri = "http://127.0.0.1:18765/v1"
#   api_key = "dummy"
#   [agents.repro]
#   enabled = true
#   model_provider = "openai.mock"
#   risk_profile = "default"
#   runtime_profile = "default"
#   [risk_profiles.default]
#   [runtime_profiles.default]
#   [cost]
#   daily_limit_usd = 0.01
#   [cost.enforcement]
#   mode = "warn"
#   [cost.rates.providers.models.openai."mock-model"]
#   input_per_mtok = 100.0
#   output_per_mtok = 100.0
#   cached_input_per_mtok = 100.0

zeroclaw --config-dir ./cfg agent -a repro -m "hi"   # turn 1: "ok", records $1.0005
zeroclaw --config-dir ./cfg agent -a repro -m "hi"   # turn 2: refused, see the log below
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone who prices their models (`[cost.rates]`, legacy `pricing`, or `live_pricing`) and leaves `mode` at its documented default, `warn`.
Frequency: always, once a limit is crossed.
Consequence:
- The agent stops answering for the rest of the day or month, on every channel that runs in the budget scope.
- An operator who chose `warn`, or kept the default, has no reason to expect that.
- `block` and `route_down` can't be told apart from `warn`; `route_down` in particular never substitutes the model.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
=== turn 1
ok
exit=0
=== turn 2
Error: Budget exceeded: $1.0005 of $0.01 Day limit. Cannot make further API calls until the budget resets.
exit=1
=== mock POSTs: 1
```

### ZeroClaw version

zeroclaw 0.9.0 (6c78ba5), release binary x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu. The code path is unchanged on master `3a3f2e3586`.

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)

### Operating system

Fedora-based Linux x86_64

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

Once a session hits `cost.daily_limit_usd`, every later turn fails, and the only way to continue is to raise the limit and restart the daemon. Restarting kills every live session. Two separate gaps cause this.

**`allow_override` does nothing.** [`CostConfig::allow_override`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs#L7393) is documented as "Allow requests to exceed budget with --override flag", but no flag, RPC method or client action reads it. Outside schema defaults and one gateway test, nothing in the tree references it. When the budget is exceeded, [`enforce_tool_loop_budget`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/provider_call.rs#L211) fails the turn with an error string, and ZeroCode shows it as an ordinary failed turn. The user gets no prompt and no way to continue.

**Raising the limit from ZeroCode does not reach the running tracker.** The daemon builds the process-global `CostTracker` [once at startup](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/daemon/mod.rs#L1107), and RPC turns use that handle directly ([`dispatch.rs#L6656`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L6656)). [`save_and_swap_config`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L3097) swaps the live `Config` but never calls [`CostTracker::update_config`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/cost/tracker.rs#L257). The tracker therefore keeps the old limits until some other path calls `get_or_init_global` with a fresh config. ACP turns do this [per turn](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/acp_server.rs#L2008); ZeroCode's RPC turns do not. The tracker's own docs say reloads apply "at the next check_budget", which holds only for those other paths.

Related: `cost.enforcement.mode` defaults to `"warn"` and accepts `"block"` and `"route_down"`, but no runtime code reads it. The budget check always blocks. That is out of scope here; I note it because it is a second advertised escape hatch that does not exist.

### Expected behavior

- When a turn would exceed a daily or monthly limit, ZeroCode shows a blocking notice in red. The notice names the period, the recorded spend and the limit, and stays up until the user acts on it.
- With `allow_override = true`, the notice offers "override and continue". This lifts enforcement for the rest of the current period in the running daemon. No restart is needed and no session is lost. The override ends when the period rolls over. With `allow_override = false`, the notice explains how to raise the limit instead.
- Changing `cost.*` through `config/set` takes effect at the next budget check on every path, RPC turns included.
- Hard-limit enforcement is unchanged for channels without an interactive client (Telegram, cron, webhooks).

The warning-threshold half of this flow is #10950. Its notice should use the same red, must-dismiss presentation.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. [cost] daily_limit_usd = 300, allow_override = true. Run the daemon and a ZeroCode session until recorded spend passes $300.
2. Observe: the turn fails with "Budget exceeded: $303.5080 of $300.00 Day limit". There is no prompt and no override action.
3. In ZeroCode's config editor, set cost.daily_limit_usd = 800. config.toml now shows 800.
4. Send another prompt in the same session.
5. Observe: it fails again against the $300 limit. Only a daemon restart picks up 800.
```

### Impact

A user who hits the limit mid-task has to restart the daemon, which drops every open session, including sessions with turns in flight. `allow_override` suggests a recovery path that does not exist, so the user looks for an override and does not find one.

### Logs / stack traces

Runtime trace from the dogfood daemon (revision below), local time +08:00. The reject at 06:08:57 came after `config.toml` was rewritten with `daily_limit_usd = 800` at 06:08:34:

```text
06:06:41  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:07:40  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:08:13  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:08:57  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:09:15  Received SIGINT, shutting down...
```

### ZeroClaw version

Observed on `3541e272540590f58f8a9085c800c10690fc04bb` (dogfood integration build). Source paths cited at master `e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d`, where the same code is present.

### Rust version

Not collected; no build for this report.

### Operating system

macOS (arm64). The paths involved are not OS-specific.

### Regression?

No. `allow_override` has never been wired.

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. Observed on the dogfood build above; master was checked by source reading.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: PowerShell dialect rejects any command with a bare `@` in an argument (allowlisted mail CLI unusable)
issues.body:
﻿**Component:** `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs` (`split_powershell_pipeline_syntax`, `validate_command_execution_for_shell`)
**Version:** 0.8.6 (`c473221`), Windows x86_64, `runtime.shell` unset (runtime picks the PowerShell dialect)
**Labels (suggested):** bug, security-policy, regression, windows

---

## Summary

After upgrading 0.8.5 → 0.8.6 any allowlisted command whose argument contains a bare `@` is rejected
before the risk gate runs. For us this killed outbound mail: `himalaya message compose --to user@example.com …`
fails with `Command not allowed by security policy`, while the same command without `--to`, `echo test --send`,
and `himalaya envelope list` all pass.

Toggling `block_high_risk_commands` has no effect — the gate is a different one, which made the
diagnosis misleading: the error text points at the allowlist, not at command parsing.

## Root cause

`split_powershell_pipeline_syntax` treats `@` as an expression introducer anywhere in an unquoted token:

```rust
';' | '\r' | '\n' | '&' | '(' | ')' | '{' | '}' | '[' | ']' | '<' | '>' | '@' => {
    return None;
}
```

Returning `None` makes `validate_command_execution_for_shell` fail the *allowlist* gate:

```
Command not allowed by security policy: himalaya message compose --to user@example.com --body x
```

`block_high_risk_commands` is checked later, so turning it off cannot help. `is_command_explicitly_allowed`
is never reached either.

## Reproduction

Config: `risk_profiles.<alias>.allowed_commands = ["dir", "echo", "date", "himalaya"]`,
`require_approval_for_medium_risk = true`, `block_high_risk_commands = true` (and identically with `false`),
`autonomy = supervised`. Agent runs these through the `shell` tool:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `himalaya envelope list --page-size 1` | ok |
| `himalaya message compose --help` | ok |
| `himalaya message compose --body "test"` | ok |
| `himalaya message compose --to user@example.com --body test` | **`Command not allowed by security policy`** |
| `himalaya message compose --to user@example.com --subject s --body test --send` | **same** |
| `echo test --send` | ok |

Confirmed on a stand `--config-dir` with 0.8.6; reproducible with any binary that takes an address argument
(`himalaya`, `git` with `@{…}` refs, `curl` URLs containing `@`, `docker run image@sha256:…`).

## Why this is not only over-blocking, but also misleading

`@` inside quotes is accepted by the same tokenizer (`QuoteState::Double` path), so
`himalaya message compose --to "user@example.com" --send` is *not* blocked by this gate. The check therefore
does not restrict data egress through mail clients — it only punishes commands where the address is unquoted.
Pretending it is an anti-exfiltration control would be wrong; it is an accident of PowerShell expression parsing.

## Expected behaviour

An `@` that is not at the start of a token, and not followed by `(`, `{`, or an identifier that begins a
splat, is plain text inside an argument. Only real expression forms should invalidate the command:

* `@(` — array subexpression
* `@{` — hashtable
* `@name` — splatting (start of token)

Suggested change in the tokenizer: treat `@` as a terminator only when it is the first character of a token,
or when followed by `(` / `{`. Everything else should be accumulated into `token_body` like ordinary text.

If the maintainers prefer keeping the strict grammar, the second-best option is to reject with a message that
names the real gate (e.g. `Command rejected: '@' cannot be parsed in the PowerShell dialect, quote the
argument`) — the current text sent us to `allowed_commands` and `block_high_risk_commands` for two hours.

## What we had to do instead

We could not keep calling `himalaya` from `shell` at all, so we now route agent mail through a wrapper
(`mail`) that takes a **recipient key** from a human-owned whitelist and resolves the address itself:
the address never appears on the command line, the wrapper validates it, and an unknown key produces a draft
without a recipient instead of a send. That works, but it is a workaround for a parser limitation, and it
moved recipient validation out of ZeroClaw into our own script.

## Ask

1. Fix the `@` handling in `split_powershell_pipeline_syntax` as described (preferred).
2. Failing that, an opt-in knob for the PowerShell tokenizer, or a distinct error class, so that a policy
   author can tell "unknown command" from "argument cannot be parsed".
3. Consider documenting, for `risk_profiles.*.allowed_commands`, that the PowerShell dialect imposes an
   argument grammar on top of the command allowlist — `allowed_commands = ["himalaya"]` is not sufficient
   to run `himalaya` with flags, which is not obvious from the schema description
   ("command names, not subcommands").

## Related

* #11058 — the `allowed_commands` exemption from `block_high_risk_commands` is still present in 0.8.6
  (`is_command_explicitly_allowed_for_shell`), so it is **not** the cause here: our command never reaches
  the risk gate at all.
* #11799 — same symptom family: the refusal text names the wrong source of the decision. Here it says
  "not allowed by security policy" while the command *is* allowlisted.

issues.body:
### Task

Make `dashboard_core::tests::a_chat_whose_reply_end_cannot_be_written_ends` (crates/zeroclaw-gateway) pass on Windows, or limit it to the platforms where its premise holds.

### Context

The test was added in #12244. It shrinks the socket buffers at both ends so that a reply's final frame can't be written, then expects the chat to close its conversation at the write deadline. PR CI runs no Windows tests. The scheduled Platform Tests on master fail on Windows every run, starting with the first run after #12244 merged. That includes run 42952365996 on 1a79f89d1e and the run on the v0.9.0 release commit 6c78ba59bc:

```
FAIL [  32.623s] zeroclaw-gateway dashboard_core::tests::a_chat_whose_reply_end_cannot_be_written_ends
thread 'dashboard_core::tests::a_chat_whose_reply_end_cannot_be_written_ends' panicked at crates\zeroclaw-gateway\src\dashboard_core.rs:2417:13:
a chat that could not write its reply's end closes its conversation: still live: ["647b7f83-20bc-4c75-8c33-e74d7387a76b"]
```

Likely cause, not yet reproduced: Windows sockets accept writes beyond a small `SO_SNDBUF`/`SO_RCVBUF`. If so, the final write completes, and the conversation stays live because the client socket is still open, which is correct. If that's right, product behavior is unchanged and only the test's premise fails on Windows.

### Acceptance criteria

- On Windows, either the stuck write is forced another way, or the test is gated to non-Windows targets with the reason in a comment.
- The scheduled Windows Platform Tests job no longer reports this test.
- If a reproduction shows the write deadline is not enforced on Windows, file that as a separate bug.

### Likely files or areas

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/dashboard_core.rs` (the test near line 5973 and its `serve_with_small_send_buffers` / `open_chat_with_small_receive_buffer` helpers)

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

Reviewers of #12244

### Risk notes

Test-only. It doesn't affect released binaries.

issues.title: [Bug]: remove() of a plugin whose directory is gone fails on Windows because rename_new loses ErrorKind::NotFound
issues.body:
### Affected component

plugins

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`Scheduled Platform Tests` fails this test on Windows in every run I checked, from
2026-10-31 through the latest. From run 43672109720 (2026-11-15, sha `3a3f2e358`),
job 132684326490:

```text
FAIL [   0.039s] ( 8373/19974) zeroclaw-plugins host::tests::remove_of_a_package_whose_directory_is_gone_keeps_what_is_at_its_name

  thread 'host::tests::remove_of_a_package_whose_directory_is_gone_keeps_what_is_at_its_name' (1048) panicked at crates\zeroclaw-plugins\src\host.rs:7935:32:
  called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Io(Custom { kind: Other, error: Error { code: HRESULT(0x80070002), message: "The system cannot find the file specified." } })
```

Column 32 of `host.rs:7935` is the `.unwrap()` on `host.remove("weather")`: the
remove itself returns an error on Windows. Runs seen failing: 41163968617 (2026-10-31,
job 124428177957), 41382873404 (2026-11-02, job 125077417459), 41766659979 (11-04),
42333577353 (11-07) and 43672109720 (11-15). The test came in with `02bb07526`
(#11809, 2026-10-22).

The failure and its `HRESULT(0x80070002)` were first listed, without a cause, in a
downstream report on #7461 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7461#issuecomment-6716042569).

### Expected behavior

`remove()` of a loaded package whose directory is already gone succeeds, clears the
loaded entry, sweeps its hidden transaction entry, and leaves an unrelated directory at
the package name untouched. That is what the Linux job does and what the test asserts.

### Root cause

The Windows leg of the package move erases the error kind. `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/host/recovery.rs:440-475`:

```rust
#[cfg(windows)]
fn rename_new(from: &Dir, name: &str, to: &Dir, dest: &str) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    ...
    unsafe { MoveFileW(PCWSTR(source.as_ptr()), PCWSTR(destination.as_ptr())) }
        .map_err(std::io::Error::other)
}
```

`std::io::Error::other` always yields `ErrorKind::Other`, so a `MoveFileW` failure
that means "the source is not there" arrives as `kind: Other` carrying the raw
`HRESULT(0x80070002)`, exactly as in the panic message above.

`remove_with_report` has an arm written for precisely this case, `host.rs:789-794`:

```rust
// Already gone, so nothing is left to delete.
Err(PluginError::Io(error)) if error.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
    self.loaded.remove(name);
    finish_naming_entry(&self.plugins_dir, root, held)?;
    return Ok(Vec::new());
}
```

It matches on `ErrorKind::NotFound`, which the Windows path can never produce:

* On Linux `rename_new` goes through
  `rustix::fs::renameat_with(..., RenameFlags::NOREPLACE)` and `std::io::Error::from(Errno)`,
  so `ENOENT` becomes `ErrorKind::NotFound` and the arm fires.
* On Windows the same condition comes back as `ErrorKind::Other`, the arm is skipped,
  `Err(error)` is returned, and the test's `unwrap()` panics.

So this is a Windows behaviour bug, not only a bad test: on Windows a remove of a
package whose directory disappeared outside the host fails instead of cleaning up the
host's own state. `rename_new` is also what `claim` and `publish` call
(`recovery.rs:322` and `:328`), so any other caller that branches on the kind of their
error has the same blind spot on Windows. I have only traced the `remove` path.

### Steps to reproduce

```powershell
git checkout 3a3f2e358
$env:CARGO_TARGET_DIR = "C:\zc-target"
cargo test -p zeroclaw-plugins remove_of_a_package_whose_directory_is_gone_keeps_what_is_at_its_name
# as CI runs it:
cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-plugins remove_of_a_package_whose_directory_is_gone_keeps_what_is_at_its_name
```

### Impact

The `Platform Test (Windows)` job is masked with
`continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.name == 'Windows' }}`, so nothing is blocked. The cost is
that `remove` is wrong on Windows for any package whose directory went away outside the
host (an editor sync, an antivirus quarantine, a manual cleanup), and that the error
kinds this module reasons about are unreliable on Windows.

### Possible fix

Map the Win32 failure to an `ErrorKind` instead of flattening it, keeping the HRESULT
in the payload. A sketch, not compiled:

```rust
use windows::Win32::Foundation::{ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS, ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND, ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND};

unsafe { MoveFileW(PCWSTR(source.as_ptr()), PCWSTR(destination.as_ptr())) }.map_err(|error| {
    let code = error.code();
    let kind = if code == ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.to_hresult() || code == ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND.to_hresult() {
        std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound
    } else if code == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS.to_hresult() {
        std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists
    } else {
        std::io::ErrorKind::Other
    };
    std::io::Error::new(kind, error)
})
```

I have no Windows machine to hand, so this is read from source and from the CI log
and has not been run: the mapping needs a Windows check, including which code
`MoveFileW` returns for an existing destination.

A regression test that pins the kind would hold it in place, e.g. in the existing
`#[cfg(all(test, windows))] mod windows_tests` (`recovery.rs:963`): move a name that
does not exist and assert `rename_new(...).unwrap_err().kind() == ErrorKind::NotFound`.
That assertion cannot pass today.

### ZeroClaw version

master @ `3a3f2e358`

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)

### Operating system

`windows-latest` GitHub-hosted runner (the `windows-tar` nextest matrix leg)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup: the test has failed on Windows since it was added in `02bb07526`
(#11809).

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

prs.title: feat(providers): adopt the canonical V5 registry and runtime model bindings
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`; merge only after the dependencies below.
- **What changed and why:** Activate canonical registry admission and backend consumers, promote V4 configuration to V5, materialize complete models for routing/fallback/switching, and wire secret-safe registry editing. Registry types, native protocols, chat transport and reflection are prepared in #12454, #12455, #12456 and #12457.
- **Scope boundary:** V5 admission, persistence/editor wiring, canonical model construction and backend consumer/lifecycle cutover. Activation and affected consumers remain together so no intermediate revision clears profiles that active consumers still read. Zerocode and Web follow separately.
- **Blast radius:** Config persistence and secret handling; provider construction; agent/session lifecycle; memory, speech and decision consumers; channel/gateway/RPC dispatch.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related to #9809. Stack part 9; reference implementation `921b8ee993a0b2439a0c2c41cb84337270942a06`. Depends on #12457.

### What this does, simply

The preceding layers prepare independent registry types, native capability protocols, chat transport and generic reflection. This layer activates those components: V4 input is promoted at the V5 admission boundary, backend consumers resolve exact model references, and routing, fallback and switching build complete target bindings. Configuration activation and dependent consumers stay together to avoid a partially switched runtime. This remaining cutover is still large; the preparatory layers make their own architectural boundaries independently reviewable.

## Testing (required)


### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes` — the migration or interactive workflow below supplements passing current-head CI.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** Requested surface: `cli`. Not exercised interactively at this revision.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Check out this head with its parent commits; use the repository toolchain and existing test fixtures.
- **Steps to run:** Run workspace Quality Gate, migration and registry edit tests, provider protocol tests, runtime route/switch/fallback/refresh tests and feature-matrix checks; exercise `zeroclaw config migrate` with a V4 backup.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** V4 configuration becomes V5 connections/models; internal consumers resolve exact model keys; switching/fallback materializes all target configuration and a failed update preserves the previous binding.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Master stores provider-owned profiles and consumer-specific capability settings, and has no canonical decoupled registry.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [Current-head CI](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/43691399717) passes `CI Required Gate`, workspace tests, opt-in tool tests, lint, security, and the applicable feature/platform build checks at `b46ac874c036def0c6da63856eb0200492c8ec5f`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The separate PR-risk reporter failed its head-bound evidence capture. Live CLI/migration verification remains pending; passing CI does not establish the two old-configuration migration restrictions identified in review. Original #9809 CI does not validate intermediate stack revisions.
- **Commands run and tail output:** `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: exit 0, no formatting diff. `git diff --check`: exit 0, no whitespace errors.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Addressed previous-head split dependency errors (retained embedding factory, complete timeout helpers, deferred dispatch-dependent sampling, and secret-test trait import). New-head execution remains pending. Compared the integrated provider and UI trees byte-for-byte with the saved pre-split snapshot. Preserved the frozen V4 fixture. Corrected previous-head CI failures caused by unnecessary TOML rewriting; the existing comment-preservation and atomic-save assertions remain intact. New-head execution is pending. Inspected ownership, imports and the incremental diff against the parent. Runtime/network behavior has not been re-executed locally.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Pending: CLI Quickstart and configuration command output require exact-head verification before interface sign-off.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `b46ac874c036def0c6da63856eb0200492c8ec5f`; source formatting only.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** No interactive action performed; current-head CI passed, while manual runtime checks remain pending.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Local Cargo build/test/clippy were intentionally skipped at the author’s request to use GitHub CI instead of repeated heavy local compilation.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes; existing capability selection is represented in the new registry. Existing admission boundaries remain in force.
- New external network calls? Yes; native capability adapters use the selected connection and protocol. No additional allowlist bypass is introduced.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes; connection credentials and sensitive headers use the existing encrypted persistence and masked edit contracts.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes; shared extraction policy is selected per materialized model.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Migration, registry editing and provider selection cross configuration trust boundaries. Preserve ciphertext, use masked compare-and-swap edits, validate references before installation, and keep the previous binding when construction fails. Provider output remains subject to runtime tool admission.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Older files are converted at the migration boundary; the new internal API and persisted V5 shape replace profile-owned construction.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes; connections, models, presets, fallback references and configuration editing use the V5 shape.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: Back up the existing configuration and run `zeroclaw config migrate`. Inspect the resulting connections/models and exact model references. V1-V3 first migrate through the frozen V4 step, then V4-to-V5. Install the dependent clients before the complete interactive rollout; restore the V4 backup for a V4 downgrade.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert merged children before this layer. Restore the pre-upgrade V4 backup when returning to a V4 binary; retain memory identity checks and never downgrade by editing only the version number.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None added for staging the stack.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** CI compile errors, configuration load failures, or changed provider behavior in the layer-specific regression tests.

Stack integration: this repository grants this author read-only access. These fork PRs therefore target `master` and have cumulative diffs. Review the incremental layer against its declared parent; merge parents first and refresh each child before merging. Original #9809 remains the reference PR and is not superseded or closed.

prs.title: fix(runtime): stop hard-coding temperature in the heartbeat decision and the model-routing probe
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **Two internal calls always sent `temperature = 0.0`, whatever the configured model accepts:**
    - the heartbeat's phase-1 decision turn (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/daemon/mod.rs`);
    - the model-routing tool's liveness probe (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/model_routing_config.rs`).
  - **Models that reject a sampling temperature refuse it with HTTP 400** ("temperature is deprecated for this model"); current Opus models are examples.
    - Phase 1 then fails on every tick and falls back to running every task.
    - The probe's 400 isn't retryable, so the tool reverts the default model it just saved.
  - **Both calls now send what that agent's or alias's turns send:** its configured provider temperature, or none, so the provider's default applies.
    - For the heartbeat, phases 1 and 2 now read it from one helper.
    - Phase 1's turn moves into a small helper, `heartbeat_decision_turn`, so a test can drive it.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No provider change, and no per-model rule.
  - Turns with a configured temperature send it as before.
  - The skill review fork's equivalent is #12363, and isn't touched here.
  - The temperature the Anthropic provider sets itself when native thinking is on is a separate question, raised in the linked issue.
- **Blast radius:**
  - **Heartbeat phase 1, when no temperature is configured:** the decision turn now uses the provider's default sampling instead of 0.0, as phase 2's task turns already do. The decision prompt carries the current time, so it was never a repeatable request anyway.
  - **The routing probe:** it now sends the alias's configured temperature, so a temperature the model rejects fails the probe as it would fail the alias's turns.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #12366. Related #12362 / #12363 (the same class in the skill review fork), #6095, #6147, #6144, #6598 (the May per-model omission for Opus 4.7), #6848 (the refactor that replaced it with optional temperature end to end).

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw only sends a sampling temperature when one is configured; otherwise the model provider uses its own default. That's deliberate. Some models refuse any temperature, and leaving it out is what lets them work.

Two internal requests ignored that rule and always sent a temperature of 0:
- **The heartbeat's quick "which tasks should run now?" question.** On a model that refuses it, that question failed on every tick, so every task ran every time.
- **The check the model-routing tool makes before switching the default model.** On such a model it failed, and the tool undid the switch.

Both now send exactly what the agent's normal turns send. Nothing changes for anyone who configured a temperature.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The two new tests drive the real turn and the real probe against a local Messages API and check the request body. A live check needs an API key for a model that rejects temperature.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** none user-facing beyond the daemon's heartbeat and the `model_routing_config` tool.
- **Setup / preconditions:** none.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required Rust checks (fmt, clippy, the runtime and tools tests) cover both changed files.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none.
- **Commands run and tail output:** on Linux x86_64, Rust 1.98.0:

  ```text
  cargo fmt --all -- --check                                   # clean
scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                           # Comment hygiene gate passed.
git diff --check master..HEAD                                # clean
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-tools --all-targets -- -D warnings
                                                             # 0 warnings
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- --exact daemon::tests::heartbeat_decision_turn_sends_only_the_configured_temperature
                                                             # 1 passed (3 runs)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-tools --lib -- --exact model_routing_config::tests::probe_model_sends_only_the_configured_temperature
                                                             # 1 passed (3 runs)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- daemon:: heartbeat::  # 155 passed, 1 ignored (daemon 108, heartbeat 47)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-tools --lib -- model_routing_config::  # 41 passed
  ```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - **New tests:**
    - **`daemon::tests::heartbeat_decision_turn_sends_only_the_configured_temperature`:** runs phase 1's decision turn for an agent on `claude-opus-5-5` against a local Messages API. It checks that the request has no `temperature` when none is configured, and `0.25` when `0.25` is.
    - **`model_routing_config::tests::probe_model_sends_only_the_configured_temperature`:** the same for `probe_model`, with `0.4`.
  - **Revert check:** putting back only the `Some(0.0)` argument fails each test.

    ```text
    # heartbeat_decision_turn back to Some(0.0):
assertion `left == right` failed: the decision turn must send the configured temperature (None), and none when unset: {...}
  left: Some(Number(0.0))
 right: None
# probe_model back to Some(0.0):
assertion `left == right` failed: the probe must send the configured temperature (None), and none when unset: {...}
  left: Some(Number(0.0))
 right: None
    ```

  - **Swept:** no other production call site hard-codes a temperature on `master`. The other literal values are in tests.
  - **Not verified:** a live run against Anthropic's API. The 400 itself is from #12362's and #6095's reports.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A, no user-visible interface state changed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** no web, gateway or provider checks, because nothing there changed.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No.
- New external network calls? No.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. The fixtures use synthetic keys and a loopback server.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert` of either commit restores the old fixed `0.0` at that site.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.
